Baselane Review: How to Stop Landlord Burnout From Costing You $800,000+

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that rental property is how I broke free.
  • I’ve had good tenants, great tenants, and tenants who refused to take their trash with them during the final walkthrough.
  • I’m forever grateful for owning rental property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rental property is how I broke free. The rent from my San Francisco properties was one of the foundations that let me leave banking in 2012 at age 34. Without it, I’d probably still be waking up at 5 am to get to the office by 5:45 am and leaving after 6 pm.

I’ve been a landlord since 2005. I’ve had good tenants, great tenants, and tenants who refused to take their trash with them during the final walkthrough.

I’m forever grateful for owning rental property. But the older I get, the less I enjoy being a landlord.

It’s not the math. It’s the tenant headaches, the turnover, and the maintenance. The 9 pm leaky faucet text. The final walkthrough that starts 30 minutes late. At 49 with two young kids, my time is worth more and my patience is worth less.

Recent findings suggest that 2025 tested me with three tenant turnovers. Each one meant a deposit to return, walls to paint, a vacancy to absorb, and a newly introduced tenant to find. Not long after, I sold one of my rentals. Earning 100% passive income feels better.

But selling also feels like giving up. Owning rental property is a war of attrition. The longer you hold, the more wealth you usually build. Hold until you pass, and your heirs may get a step-up in basis that wipes out the capital gains entirely.

Selling isn’t free either. Commissions, transfer taxes, capital gains, and depreciation recapture take a significant bite. Then you lose the rent check and future appreciation on a property you’ll likely never buy back at the same price.

Semi-passive income you can live with beats optimized income you can’t wait to dump. You can’t automate away a difficult tenant or a burst pipe. But you can automate a lot of what surrounds them. That’s where Baselane comes in.

For 21 years, I’ve tracked my rental finances with a spreadsheet and emails. Old school. With three rentals left in San Francisco, it kind of works. I know my numbers, more or less.

According to recent reports, but add another property, an LLC, a partner, or a short-term rental, and a DIY system starts to creak. Debits and credits slip through the cracks.

Four rentals is why I sold one last year. I couldn’t comfortably handle all the maintenance and management myself. And I didn’t want to pay a property manager 10% of rent or more to do a worse job than me.

In a recent development, since Baselane is sponsoring this post, I opened a free account for one of my SF rentals to see how it compares. Here’s what stood out.

Recent findings suggest that baselane is a free business bank account, bookkeeping software, and rent collection app rolled into one login, built for landlords. Think business checking plus QuickBooks plus Venmo for rent, except it knows what a Schedule E is.

According to recent reports, banking and books live in the same system, so you never reconcile. Baselane is a fintech, not a bank. Deposits are held at Thread Bank, Member FDIC.

Recent findings suggest that one of the first rules of landlording is to keep rental money separate from personal money. One of the second rules is that it gets messy fast once you own more than one property.

With Baselane, you can open unlimited checking and savings accounts under one login. One per property, one per LLC, one for reserves, however you actually run your portfolio. There are no monthly maintenance fees and no minimum balances, which matters once you're running a handful of accounts.

Sources indicate that you can also matter physical and virtual debit cards with spending limits. If you pay contractors, cleaners, or a handyman, you can hand someone a card capped at, say, $1,500 for materials instead of fronting cash and chasing receipts.

In a recent development, the reserve accounts earn interest. Right now 2.88%. Letting a five-figure repair reserve sit in a checking account earning nothing is a donation to your bank.

Sources indicate that if you try it, start with one property. Move its rent and its bills over, get comfortable, then decide about the rest.

Plenty of banks let you open separate accounts. What's different here is that every transaction gets tagged to a property and a Schedule E category as it happens.

In a recent development, here's why that matters. Before my old Marina tenants moved in, I spent about $2,500 and many hours fixing up the yard. They agreed to hire a gardener twice a month. They never did. Before they moved out, I paid my landscaper $1,400 including materials to restore it, plus two days of my own labor.

Those are deductible repair and maintenance expenses. But only if you record them against the right property and can find the receipts a year later. With one property, I can do that myself. With five, it becomes a part-time job.

On the Smart strategy, you set rules once, like “payments to my landscaper go to the SF rental under Repairs,” and an AI assistant handles the rest. You can snap a photo of a receipt and it matches it to the transaction.

Industry observers note that this is the part that speaks to my real pain point: tenant headaches. It is also my favorite reason for using Baselane.

I rented my Marina house to five tenants from 2015 to 2017 for about $8,200 a month. The lease charged a $250 late fee after the 4th. Rent was late eight times in 24 months. I waived the fee every single time.

That’s $2,000 I left on the table because I’m a softie who dislikes confrontation. Their method of paying was walking into my bank branch and depositing directly into my account. One July 4th weekend, rent demonstrated up on the 10th. That’s difficult to deal with when my mortgage is due by the 5th of each month, resulting in cash flow challenges.

That awkwardness wore me down. In 2017, I sold the Marina house for about $2.75 million to simplify my life.

It has been revealed that thanks to the AI boom pushing San Francisco prices higher, that house is likely worth $800,000 to $1 million more today. Sure, I reinvested the proceeds, so the true opportunity cost is lower. But it still stings.

If I’d had a system to collect rent, send reminders, and enforce late fees without me playing bad cop, I would have held on. Selling out of fatigue can be one of the most expensive decisions a landlord makes.

Recent findings suggest that that’s what Baselane does. Invoices, reminders, and late fees go out on schedule. Tenants can pay by ACH or card and set up autopay. Software doesn’t feel guilty enforcing a lease you both signed. Ultimately, Baselane removes friction which increases a rental property owner’s ability to hold on and build more wealth.

After 21 years, I've also learned that 99% of tenants want as little contact with their landlord as possible. The feeling is mutual. A system that runs rent in the background means fewer awkward conversations, and fewer awkward conversations means a happier landlord who's less tempted to sell.

Two catches. Tenants who pay by card pay a 3.49% fee, so steer them to ACH. And if your current rent collection works fine, then great. Baselane's value is rent, banking, and books living in one place.

Industry observers note that if you run short-term rentals, payouts from Airbnb, Vrbo, or Booking.com can take several business days to clear at a normal bank. Across multiple listings, that's a constant gap between money earned and money available.

Baselane offers faster payouts when you use it as your deposit account on booking platforms, with each listing feeding its own account. Next-day payouts are available for free owners.

It has been revealed that A healthy bank balance doesn't mean a property is performing. You might have a big repair coming, insurance up 20%, or expenses sitting in the wrong account.

According to recent reports, I recently ran the numbers on my San Francisco rental for a post on whether to raise the rent when tenants strike it rich. Rent is $10,250 a month, roughly $1,250 below market, because I honor a three-year rent schedule capped at about 3% a year. One vacant month wipes out about eight months of that discount. And a 2.5% annual increase only covers about 80% of my rising insurance and basic maintenance costs.

According to recent reports, I know those numbers because I track them myself. Most landlords never sit down and run them.

Baselane builds income, expense, cash flow, and net operating income reports for each property or your whole portfolio, because every transaction is already tagged. No building spreadsheets from scratch.

Sources indicate that with one rental and a spreadsheet you trust, you may not need this. With several properties or LLCs, it's the difference between knowing and guessing whether a property is worth keeping.

Sources indicate that tax season is where sloppy books come back to bite. You end up gathering records, digging up receipts, and trying to remember what a charge from eight months ago was for.

Because Baselane categorizes everything during the year, you can download a tax package with Schedule E reports, income statements, and transaction ledgers with receipts for each property and entity. Then you hand it to your CPA or use it to file yourself.

Industry observers note that if you have one rental and a DIY system that works, you don't need it. But the Core plan is free, so there's little downside to trying it.

Baselane makes the most sense if you own several rentals, hold properties in LLCs, or self-manage. Property managers have quoted me fees ranging from 10% to 20% of rent. On a $10,250 rental, a 10% fee is $1,250 a month. Baselane Smart, its premium version is just $20.

That's not apples to apples. Baselane won't fix your garbage disposal or talk to your tenants. But if you self-manage, the administrative half of the job gets a lot lighter.

It has been revealed that it's also worth a look if you're on the fence about selling a rental because you're worn out. Lighten the load before you list it and pay all those exorbitant fees. And if you're buying your next property, set up clean systems first. They're easier to build with one property than to retrofit with five.

Core is free and includes unlimited accounts, debit cards with spend controls, rent collection with automated reminders and late fees, property-level tracking, and the accountant tax package.

Smart is $20 a month with a 30-day free trial and adds AI auto-tagging, receipt matching, auto-transfers to maintain target balances, faster rent deposits, and balance sheet reports.

It has been revealed that compare that to what you may already pay. Some business bank accounts charge $5 to $25 a month in maintenance fees. At $15 a month across five accounts, that's $900 a year just to keep them open. Baselane charges no maintenance fees, no minimums, and ACH transfers and incoming wires are free.

No product is perfect, and pretending otherwise insults your intelligence.

Rental property helped me break free due to the semi-passive income it generates. But a rental only builds wealth if you can stand to keep owning it.

According to recent reports, the headaches that make me want to sell are tenants, turnover, and maintenance. Baselane doesn't make those entirely disappear. What it does is take the money side of landlording, rent collection, late fees, accounts, and records, and put it on autopilot. Less friction overall means more energy for the parts that actually need a human.

In a recent development, my proposal going forward is simple. Own fewer, better rentals and make each one as close to passive as possible. Let the private real estate side of my portfolio be 100% passive. And spend the time I save being a full-time dad.

Industry observers note that if I’d had automated rent and late fees with my Marina tenants, I’d have $2,000 more and far fewer awkward conversations. I also might still own the house today. That’s at least an $800,000 lesson in letting small annoyances drive big decisions.

Sources indicate that selling a rental is permanent. Making one easier to own isn't.

In a recent development, if you own rental property and want it to feel a little more passive, check out Baselane here. The Core plan is free, so the only cost of trying it is an afternoon.

Have you ever sold a rental property because you were tired of managing it, not because the numbers stopped working? Do you regret it? What's the one landlord headache that would push you to sell: tenants, turnover, maintenance, or the paperwork? Do you track your rental finances yourself or hand them off? And have you ever waived a late fee you were fully entitled to collect?

In a recent development, what should real estate investors look for when choosing a bank? Look for property-specific accounts, integrated rent collection, automated bookkeeping, and tax prep support. Multi-property investors benefit most from platforms that organize transactions by property and entity automatically. Security deposit tracking also helps keep tenant funds clearly separated.

Can real estate investors open a business bank account online? Yes. Digital platforms like Baselane let you open accounts entirely online with no branch visit. Traditional banks may require in-person verification depending on their policies and your business structure.

Do any banking platforms for real estate investors offer high-yield savings? Digital-first platforms generally pay more on savings than traditional banks. Baselane pays a tiered APY on savings balances that exceeds the national average for business accounts. Traditional banks typically pay far less on business savings.

It has been revealed that how do integrated banking and bookkeeping platforms help with taxes? Platforms like Baselane categorize transactions by property and IRS Schedule E category throughout the year. That cuts manual work at tax time and produces Schedule E reports and transaction ledgers you can hand to your accountant or use to file yourself.

In a recent development, does Baselane support multiple properties? Yes. Baselane supports bookkeeping across multiple rental properties for U.S.-based entities, including single-member and multi-member LLCs, corporations, partnerships, and sole proprietorships. Banking and rent collection sync directly with bookkeeping, and you can connect external bank accounts and import historical transactions. See the pricing page for the full feature list.

Industry observers note that what reports can real estate investors generate? Portfolio-level and property-level reports including net operating income, net cash flow, rent roll, tenant ledger, total inflows and outflows, transaction ledger with receipts, balance sheet, Schedule E, and income statement. Reports export for your accountant, lender, or tax filing.

Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan.
  • Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character.
  • Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

The 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

Tanaka’s projected route across Taiwan.

Tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

Although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition initiative includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he looks to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

Tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

Industry observers note that his most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

In a recent development, during a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

On a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

By late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

Tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

Yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

It has been revealed that interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

#113915. An Internal Locus Of Control Makes You A Happier, Wealthier Investor

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1805 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

An Internal Locus Of Control Makes You A Happier, Wealthier Investor

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An internal locus of control is the belief that you control your outcomes and can solve problems as they come up.
  • Peter Gray, a research psychologist at Boston College argues in his new book, Restoring Childhood, that kids have become more anxious and depressed over the decades because adults took away their free play and independence.
  • And psychologists have long known that a weak internal locus of control is strongly linked to anxiety and depression.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An internal locus of control is the belief that you control your outcomes and can solve problems as they come up. An external locus of control is the belief that outside forces run your life. Luck. The economy. Your boss. Some CEO you’ve never met.

Peter Gray, a research psychologist at Boston College argues in his new book, Restoring Childhood, that kids have become more anxious and depressed over the decades because adults took away their free play and independence. Children who never get to solve their own problems never build an internal locus of control.

And psychologists have long known that a weak internal locus of control is strongly linked to anxiety and depression.

It makes sense. If you believe you have little control over what happens to you, the world feels cruel. At the extreme, you feel helpless. And when you feel helpless, darker thoughts start creeping in.

Industry observers note that as a father of young children, this hit home. As an investor, it hit my wallet. Recently, I got a $50,000 lesson in what it feels like to have zero control.

Recent findings suggest that from an investor’s point of view, the active investor has an internal locus of control. He believes his research and decisions can beat the market.

The passive investor has more of an external locus of control. He accepts that he can’t beat the market, so he buys the whole thing and lets it ride.

The irony is, despite the better feeling of being in control, most active investors underperform over time. I agree with that, which is why about 60% to 70% of my public investments are in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq.

But I have two problems with fully going passive.

First, I don’t want to earn the same returns as everybody else. I want to outperform so my family’s buying power grows faster than the masses. If not, we'll just be running in place with every other passive index investor.

Second, accepting that I have no control makes me less satisfied. I want to believe my decisions matter. So I keep a chunk of my portfolio in individual stocks. One of them was Nvidia for the past several years.

My Nvidia position was worth about $150,000 in October 2026. It’s now worth about $100,000.

About $30,000 of the decline came from the broader AI selloff. Fine. That’s the market. I can live with that.

The other $20,000 came from Jensen.

It has been revealed that first he admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. U.S. officials reportedly believe she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

It has been revealed that then the New York Times reported a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days later, Jensen resigned as the board moved to oust him. The stock dropped again.

Finding and keeping love truly is harder than getting rich.

Sources indicate that losing $50,000 is about a year and a half of food for my family of four. It’s also about a year and a half of the unsubsidized health insurance premiums we pay.

As the household’s provider, I feel like a failure for blowing up so much money. Without a steady day job, our investment returns are what keep us going. Every loss hits harder.

But mostly, I’m annoyed with myself for putting too much capital in one company.

Here’s the uncomfortable part. Blaming Jensen is the external locus of control response.

Recent findings suggest that an external locus of control means believing outside forces decide your fate. When I say “Jensen cost me $20,000,” I’m pinning my loss on a guy I’ve never met and can’t control.

Sources indicate that it may be true. But it leaves me helpless. I can’t stop the next CEO from falling for someone he shouldn’t. I can’t make a board build a succession plan. And I definitely can’t make billionaires stay faithful.

So the internal locus of control question is: what could I have controlled?

In a recent development, plenty, it turns out. I chose the position size. I chose to put about 40% of my public portfolio in individual stocks, instead of a more conservative 20% – 30% as suggested in my article, the Recommended Split Between Passive And Active Investing. I broke my own rule.

It has been revealed that jensen made the mess. I decided how much it could cost me.

Recent findings suggest that I also never priced in key man risk. Jensen ran Nvidia for 33 years and the firm had no successor ready. When one person is the company, his personal life is part of your investment. I need to bake that into my model.

In a recent development, and here’s the kicker. Going passive wouldn’t have 100% saved me. Nvidia is one of the largest holdings in both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq. My index funds got dinged too. Passive investing doesn’t remove the Jensen risk. It only dilutes it.

Since the Fed started aggressively hiking rates in 2022, real estate has gotten little love. Mortgage rates follow the 10-year Treasury yield, which shot up, and demand softened across the country. Meanwhile, the S&P 500, especially tech and AI stocks, grabbed the spotlight.

In a recent development, this Nvidia debacle reminded me why I prefer owning real estate over stocks. Living in your primary residence and having it appreciate it the background is easy.

Recent findings suggest that as a landlord, I have a high internal locus of control. I choose the tenants. I decide when to fix the roof, remodel the kitchen or replace the carpet. I set rents within the law. If the property underperforms, it’s usually on me.

And because I can make it better, I feel more confident and happier owning it.

No CEO can tank the value of my house with a bad decision in his personal life.

According to recent reports, real estate still has risks. Insurance covers the physical ones like fire and water damage, and with separate policies, earthquakes and floods. But insurance won’t protect you from a local recession, a spike in mortgage rates or a shift in rent laws.

Your property can absolutely lose value. It just won’t drop 20% in a week because one person made a bad decision.

Industry observers note that sure, real estate may only appreciate 3% to 5% a year compared to roughly 10% for the S&P 500. But with 20% down, 4% appreciation is a 20% return on your equity before costs.

Sources indicate that plus you collect rent every month, and that rent doesn’t shrink the property’s value the way a dividend shrinks a organization’s cash pile. In this regard, rental income is superior to dividend income.

The older I get, the more I value steady over spectacular. I’d rather not watch $20,000 vanish in a few days.

Industry observers note that here’s the funny thing. Say it turned out I was the International Personal Finance Playboy of the World, with multiple girlfriends and a dozen kids like Elon Musk. As an Asian American, I'd be crucified and it would be a scandal in the personal finance community.

If Financial Samurai were a publicly traded penny stock, the shares might drop. Then again, bad PR is still PR. Some media outlets might cover it, traffic would surge and the stock would probably go up.

Recent findings suggest that but my real estate wouldn’t care either way. However bad a husband or father I might be, my properties won’t lose value because of my behavior. As an an investor, that's a beautiful thing.

Industry observers note that the only ways my real estate goes down are if the local economy turns or I neglect the properties and stop keeping tenants happy and rents at market. Both are mostly in my control.

So real estate remains my favorite asset class for building wealth. It provides necessary shelter and generates a lot more income than dividends to help you break free from work sooner.

For the playboys and playgirls out there, it might be even more valuable.

Industry observers note that now for the contradiction. The older and wealthier I get, the less I want to be the landlord dealing with leaky toilets and tenant turnovers. I’ve been slowly selling physical rentals and reinvesting in private real estate for more passive income.

Doesn’t that mean giving up control? Yes.

It has been revealed that but I’ve realized control was never the whole point. What I really want to avoid is single-person risk. A diversified pool of rental homes can't be taken down by a single person. One bad tenant or one bad house doesn’t sink it. You still have to trust the fund manager, so do your homework there too.

The healthiest locus of control is neither fully internal nor fully external. Control what you can: your savings rate, your asset allocation, your position sizes and the properties you choose to own. Then accept what you can’t, without feeling helpless.

Peter Gray’s point is that kids build an internal locus of control by doing hard things on their own: playing, exploring, failing and figuring it out without an adult hovering.

Industry observers note that investing works the same way. You build confidence by making decisions, owning the results and adjusting. Losing $50,000 in Nvidia this rapidly stings. But if it forces me to size positions better, it’ll make me a better investor over time.

Kids learn the same lesson in a different way. That’s one reason I want mine helping with tenant turnovers and rental property maintenance. Patching a wall, helping me do landscaping projects, and seeing a rental get leased teaches them that their effort changes outcomes.

Sometimes it’s nice to outsource your financial and parenting duties to competent people. Just make sure they’re actually competent.

The last thing you want is to pay someone for worse results than you could have gotten yourself.

How much of your portfolio is in individual stocks, and have you ever lost significant because of one executive’s behavior? Does owning real estate make you feel more in control, or more stressed? Do you factor key man risk into founder-led companies? And for the parents out there, are you giving your kids enough room to develop an internal locus of control?

AI may be the next general-purpose technology, but compute needs physical buildings and power. One way to get exposure without owning a single chip stock is through private real estate and venture.

It has been revealed that check out Fundrise, which invests in residential and industrial real estate and private AI companies. No CEO scandal can sink a diversified portfolio of properties. Fundrise is a long-time sponsor of Financial Samurai.

#113914. Tech Report: Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

📅 31 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1865 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest.
  • It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort.
  • Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

In a recent development, the expedition itself came from a merger of two plans. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

The Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times.

The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

In total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

According to recent reports, the Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia.

Base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later mentioned it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

Sources indicate that the Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

The 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com.

Sources indicate that on April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

Industry observers note that A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

It has been revealed that major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

According to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

It has been revealed that dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt said that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

“What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he remarked. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

According to recent reports, mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but mentioned that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

It has been revealed that norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com.

Industry observers note that after the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They remarked that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

Many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group said the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

Sources indicate that mazeaud’s radio message noted that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

Sources indicate that according to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later noted that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Recent findings suggest that haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He stated they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

Roberts later mentioned weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Sources indicate that roberts said that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

It has been revealed that haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He remarked that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

Recent findings suggest that uemura stated that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

Axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt said the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

Industry observers note that the problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original strategy of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth stated the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

Industry observers note that in their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

Memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

Recent findings suggest that the questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

#113912. Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3382 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3382 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that “This is absolute madness,” said a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England.
  • The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.
  • When Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “This is absolute madness,” said a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England. In a scene that couldn’t be more different from the past 28 years that he has spent walking around the world, Bushby stood underneath a giant Welcome Home Karl sign, made an appreciative speech, then begged off to continue walking the final few steps to his mother’s house, which he left back in 1998.

The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.

When Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different. Bushby was 29 years old. He is now 57. When he began, he had around $500 in his pocket, a two-wheeled cart loaded with supplies, and an idea that most people would have dismissed as a fantasy. He was going to walk home to Hull, England, without using any transport. He would not return to the UK until he could do so on foot. He expected the expedition to take about 12 years. Instead, it has taken 28.

Bushby has spent more than 10,000 days and 50,000km pursuing that single objective. The Goliath Expedition has become one of the longest and most unusual human-powered adventures in modern exploration, and he is nervous about it ending. Speaking to The Washington Post as he approached home, he said: “My purpose and reason for living is about to end. It’s going to be difficult…trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.”.

According to recent reports, through Chile’s Atacama Desert. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Industry observers note that while serving with the Parachute Regiment, Bushby received a birthday card from his father, Keith, who had served in the British Army. In it was a story about special forces soldiers debating whether it was possible to walk from London to Fresh York via the Bering Strait. Looking at a world map, Bushby began tracing the route himself.

But rather than stopping at New York, he extended the line south through the Americas, all the way to the tip of Chile. The result was an expedition that would take him from the southernmost reaches of South America back to his home in England.

“That was the moment the hairs on the back of your neck stand up,” he told GQ Magazine. “You think, well, that’s it.” He did some calculations, created a timeline on the “back of a beer mat,” and estimated the journey would take him 12 years. From that point, Bushby indicated nothing but determination. At the start, most people doubted it was even possible. That only made him more certain that he wanted to try.

In a recent development, he gave himself two rules. The first was that he could not use any transportation, even self-propelled vehicles like bicycles or kayaks, to advance the expedition. The second was that he could not return to the UK until he had completed the walk. Those rules sound simple. In practice, they created multiple logistical nightmares and affected almost every aspect of his life.

It has been revealed that 2001, the Darien Gap. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, with his equipment loaded onto a cart he calls The Beast. He was not an elite endurance athlete embarking on a carefully funded and organized expedition. He was a young former paratrooper with a few hundred dollars, a rough line on a map, and limited resources. He had no supporters or funding, and relied on gas station food or what locals gave him.

“The first years, you’re living the boys’ adventure dream, and it’s great,” he told The Upcoming York Times, “and then it really becomes a grind.”.

Industry observers note that the first few years took him north through the Americas, including multiple conflict zones. In Peru, he was attacked by a mob; in Colombia, he floated down the crocodile-laden Atrato River to avoid being spotted by armed men. Then he faced the Darien Gap, that infamously dangerous stretch between Colombia and Panama, ruled by drug and human smugglers, that almost all adventurers skirt around.

Eventually, he reached Panama. But emerging from the jungle did not mean he was free to continue. After crossing a restricted border zone without the necessary visa, he was detained for 18 days.

It has been revealed that after making his way through the Americas, Bushby eventually finished crossing the U.S., where he had picked up a few sponsorships, and reached Alaska. The next major obstacle, and the one that catapulted his journey into world news, was the Bering Strait, the stretch of water separating North America from Russia.

It has been revealed that north America. Photo: Karl Bushby.

The Arctic had already given Bushby a taste of its dangers. During the Alaskan stage of the expedition, he was rescued by helicopter after becoming stranded on an ice floe that broke away from the coast and drifted out to sea, and had a standoff with a polar bear. He knew how risky the Bering Strait crossing would be.

It has been revealed that in March 2006, Bushby and French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer spent 14 days crossing the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia on foot. With 90kg sleds, they traveled across the shifting ice in temperatures that fell to around -30˚C, against the prevailing winds as the ice moved beneath them.

Recent findings suggest that wearing dry suits, they had to swim at points through the icy, slushy water. “All night long, you’re just listening to the grinding, and the ice is just like screaming,” he told The Latest York Times. “We actually had to evacuate the tent during the night because the thing started to break apart beneath us.”.

They made it across, achieving a rare crossing of one of the world’s most formidable natural barriers. But reaching Russia did not mean the difficulties were over. Russian authorities detained the pair for entering the country without the required permission. They faced the possibility of deportation.

Crossing the Bering Strait. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Russia would consume years of Bushby’s life. He had to leave the country every 90 days because his tourist visa allowed him to stay in Russia for only 90 of every 180 days. Then in 2008, his journey came to a standstill. He lost sponsorship and could not travel to Russia for a few years. In 2011, he resumed his trek, again in 90-day stints. Then in 2012, he was denied a further visa, and in 2013, he received a five-year entry ban from Russia.

According to recent reports, here, Bushby responded with an extraordinary protest. He walked approximately 5,000km from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., hoping to draw attention to his predicament and secure the paperwork he needed to continue.

In a recent development, the years of delay exposed another unusual aspect of the expedition. Bushby’s rules did not mean he had to remain indefinitely in the country where he was stuck. Nor did they prevent him from using transport for journeys unrelated to advancing his route home. However, he couldn’t fly back to the UK during these hiatuses.

In a recent development, when visas, funding, or political restrictions prevented him from continuing, he could fly elsewhere, take a break, and wait until circumstances allowed him to resume. But he could not use that flight to skip a section of the route. Whenever he returned, he had to pick up from the exact point where he had stopped. Most of the time, he decamped to Mexico. Its lower cost of living made it a practical place to wait. He also spent time in the United States.

Bushby and Dimitri Kieffer, 2006. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Sources indicate that the distinction mattered enormously to the expedition. Bushby could board a plane to escape a logistical dead end, but when he returned to the route, he had to pick up where he had stopped. He could not simply fly over the awkward section and resume walking on the other side.

The arrangement might seem to stretch the definition of walking around the world. But for Bushby, it was the only way to maintain his two original rules without spending years of his life waiting at a closed border. Some visa delays took years to resolve. And the longer the journey continued, the harder it became to predict when, or even whether, it would end. Getting across Russia alone took almost 10 years.

He lived cheaply but still needed money to survive on this near-endless journey. Some of it came from the sponsorships he eventually acquired. During what sounded like a particularly low point 15 years ago, on one of his hiatuses in Mexico while trying to overcome another logistical hurdle on his journey, he told Backpacker magazine:.

It has been revealed that I’m 42 years old and I’m broke and I’m homeless. I’m a professional parasite. I’m a professional hobo. I’m sleeping on other people’s couches. I’m 42 years old, and I have to walk other people’s dogs, just so they’ll feed me. My job is picking up dog shit!

The passage of time is one of the most striking aspects of Bushby’s story. His expedition began in an era before smartphones, Instagram, and the expectation of sharing every stage of an adventure online. The young man who left Chile in 1998 could never have imagined that nearly three decades later, people around the world would be following his progress toward his childhood home. The fact that so many people are following it still baffles Bushby.

According to recent reports, while Bushby was away, life continued for the people he had left behind. His son, Adam, grew up, and his family had to get on with their lives without him. Adam was eight when he set off. He is now 36, with a family of his own, including a 12-year-old daughter whom Bushby has never met.

In a recent development, when his dad started the walk, Adam didn’t fully understand what was going on, or know how to explain it to people who asked. Over the years, they have tried to stay in touch and maintain some kind of relationship. At 14, Adam flew to Alaska to see his dad. It was six years after the expedition began and a turning point for him in accepting what Bushby was doing. “I did feel a bit awkward because at that point I didn’t really know my dad,” he told GQ Magazine.

Industry observers note that they later spent 10 days walking together as part of a National Geographic documentary project. Adam described the experience as surreal, suddenly stepping into his father’s world. They have spoken regularly since, but as Adam put it: “[His] life went this way, and I went that way, two separate routes.”.

Recent findings suggest that in various interviews, Adam has explained that he had nothing against his father’s ambition, that he respects what he has done and is very proud of him. But also that growing up without him had been difficult.

It has been revealed that karl Bushby has not seen other members of his family for years. He met Adam when he stepped out of the water after crossing the English Channel back to England, but he has not seen his mother in over a decade, even though he will be living with her once he arrives back at his childhood home. He recognizes how difficult the situation will be and that it is due to his choices over the last 30 years.

Recent findings suggest that “The relationship between me and my son is good, but there’s a lot to resolve there,” he told GQ Magazine. “I’ve got a granddaughter I’ve never seen, and then dear old mother, Lord. I have to live with my mother now. I’m going from a global adventure to living with my mother in a basement at 57. This is going to be a challenge.”.

Life on the road has often been lonely, but Bushby has seen kindness and hospitality in every corner of the globe. “I’ve been welcomed in by the poorest of the poor,” he told The Washington Post. “I’ve met 99.9999% of the very best of humanity. Every culture, every country, has been the same response.”.

Sources indicate that he has also had two significant romantic relationships during the expedition. He spent around seven years with a Colombian woman. Later, he had a three-year relationship with a woman from Japan. He met both while on the expedition, and it was also the reason both broke down.

After finally getting across Russia, Bushby continued through Mongolia, where he joined with other adventurers, including Angela Maxwell, to trek across the Gobi Desert with camels. After 1,130km and several disagreements, the group went their separate ways, and Busby continued into China by himself. In 2018, he crossed Kazakhstan and then made his way through Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Once again, visa issues ground the journey to a standstill. He could not get into Iran.

Industry observers note that at the same time, the world was struck down by the pandemic. More years of waiting in Mexico began, even though Bushby still had a substantial distance to cover. Eventually, in 2022, he was on the move again. Once again joined by Angela Maxwell, he did something he had never intended doing during the expedition — swimming across the Caspian Sea.

Visa issues and geopolitics meant he was unable to cross into Iran. So he came up with a upcoming blueprint. He and Maxwell went back to Uzbekistan and took a different route. They walked across the Kyzylkum Desert until they reached the Caspian Sea. A self-proclaimed terrible swimmer, he was completely outside of his comfort zone. Wearing a wetsuit and flotation equipment, he described his floating-and-swimming hybrid as floatimming. It might not have been the most elegant crossing, but after 32 days at sea, 27 of which he was swimming with Maxwell and two Azerbaijani swimmers in very choppy waters, he completed the 288km swim.

In a recent development, back on solid ground, his next job was to get across Azerbaijan and into Turkey. Here, he hit a huge milestone. He crossed the Bosphorus Bridge on May 2, 2025. This meant he was back in Europe for the first time since he started walking.

Industry observers note that the remaining distance to Britain was comparatively short, but the final stages were not straightforward. Once again, visa restrictions were the thorn in his side. Limited to traveling for 90 days at a time before having to leave Europe, he continued to use Mexico as a base as he waited for his 90 days to reset and tackled the remaining distance in short stretches.

He made it through Turkey, Bulgaria, and Romania before confronting the next issue. Bushby always knew one of the logistical challenges would be getting from France to England. He started trying to pull a strategy together. Unsurprisingly, for someone who has walked across the world, his goal was to cross it via the Channel Tunnel. The issue was that this was forbidden. He had hoped to use their service tunnel, but his request was denied.

According to recent reports, karl Bushby speaks at a civic ceremony in Hull, England earlier today. Photo: YouTube.

In a recent development, as he continued walking through Hungary and Austria, he attempted to appeal the decision, reaching out to anyone who might help, to no avail. “We have carefully considered his request and explored a range of possible options. In this instance, regretfully, we are unable to accommodate Mr Bushby’s wishes,” a spokesperson for the Eurotunnel told the BBC. This meant the only alternative was to get back into the water and swim the Channel.

It has been revealed that still walking, he had made it to Germany. Then he picked his way across Belgium and France, all the while decamping to Mexico, Canada, or the U.S. every 90 days, and trying to piece together a initiative for swimming the Channel. This proved to be another headache regarding permissions.

French rules stop anyone swimming the Channel from France to Britain. He thought he had been granted an exemption, but in September, he learned that was not the case. After much negotiation, he finally got the go-ahead. On October 5, Bushby finally landed back on British soil at Shakespeare Beach near Dover after swimming the English Channel.

Sources indicate that the crossing took three days. He spent around 20 hours in the water, spent the nights on a safety vessel, and dropped back into the water at his last-known position each morning.

Industry observers note that after 28 years abroad, he was finally back in the country he had left in 1998. But rather than feeling joy, he told The Upcoming York Times he felt a real sense of loss. After three decades on the road, the prospect of just 400km to go was hugely daunting. “I’m about to lose my purpose for living,” he noted. “It’s about to abruptly end.”.

In a recent development, he is nervous about what comes next and reintegrating into a society he no longer knows. He is considering retraining as a teacher, as he loved giving talks in schools as he walked.

One substantial question is why Bushby has become so celebrated. He is not the first person to have attempted a long-distance walk around the world. Other adventurers have spent years traveling between countries, crossing continents on foot, or undertaking journeys without motorized transport, but Bushby has singularly captured the world’s attention.

According to recent reports, karl Bushby, back turned, leaves the civic ceremony to walk the last few steps to his mother’s house. Photo: YouTube.

Recent findings suggest that it might be the particular combination of his rules, or the fact that his objective is immediately understandable. He left home, and he is walking back. There is no complicated scientific mission to explain, no specialized equipment that the public needs to understand, and no obscure record category he is aiming for. The simplicity of it gives the story an almost fable-like quality, even though the journey was not simple at all.

Recent findings suggest that with just two rules, the expedition is relatively easy to follow. Every delay matters because Bushby cannot simply skip ahead. He is forced to wait or find another solution when something blocks his route. The question becomes how he will get around it without abandoning his principles.

Industry observers note that then there is the sheer amount of time it has taken. People who first encountered Bushby’s expedition in their twenties are now well into middle age themselves. Initially, there were no updates on social media. Instead, there was the odd news article that cropped up every few years about the same man, still walking across the world. A story that seemed like an ambitious adventure morphed into an entire adult life on the road.

According to recent reports, bushby has not necessarily made the journey look enjoyable. His progress has depended as much, if not more, on navigating bureaucracy and finding support as on putting one foot in front of the other. Despite it all, he continued.

As the journey has hit an era where we can follow an adventurer’s progress in real time, every obstacle and milestone has renewed interest in the question that has followed Bushby for 28 years: Will he actually make it home?

Sources indicate that now that he has to confront a new question: How do you cope with coming home after three decades? “I will have to figure out who I am again. What is the meaning to it all? How do I find that meaning and purpose? How do I fill that hole I’m suddenly going to find myself in?” he told the BBC in the days before the expected end of the expedition. “I think the old adage goes…the only thing worse than a man who can’t fulfill his dreams is a man who’s fulfilled his dreams…because then what?”.

Deciding Between A Dream House And Millions In Anthropic Stock

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With Anthropic going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, a lot of people in San Francisco are about to face a decision they have never faced before.
  • So let's run a fun thought experiment for an “everyday millionaire” in San Francisco.
  • Option 1: A $7.5 million, 4,500 square foot, fully remodeled 5 bedroom / 5 bathroom single-family home on a large lot with views in San Francisco.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Anthropic going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, a lot of people in San Francisco are about to face a decision they have never faced before. Further, they're experiencing FOMO or regret in not investing more in Anthropic earlier.

So let's run a fun thought experiment for an “everyday millionaire” in San Francisco. You get to pick one, and only one:.

Option 1: A $7.5 million, 4,500 square foot, fully remodeled 5 bedroom / 5 bathroom single-family home on a large lot with views in San Francisco. Free and clear. Move in tomorrow.

Option 2: $8.5 million of Anthropic stock at whatever it prices at, with a six-month lockup.

My first goal is to set the line like a bookie would, splitting readers as close to 50/50 as I can.

Recent findings suggest that my second goal is to get you thinking about what the money is actually for. Follow the chain backwards. You take the job for the equity and hope there's huge upside. You want the windfall to buy a house. And you want the house because that’s where your family lives.

In a recent development, option 1 hands you the end of that chain today. No lockup, no tax bill, no waiting. That is the whole debate.

Sources indicate that you probably noticed Option 2 is worth more on paper. That is not a thumb on the scale. It is the tax code.

A house and a share of stock are not the same currency. One is an after-tax asset that throws off shelter every single day. The other is a pre-tax asset that throws off nothing at all.

To convert Anthropic stock into a $7.5 million house in California, you need $11.92 million of stock at long-term capital gains rates. That is 20% federal, plus the 3.8% net investment income tax, plus 13.3% to California. A 37.1% haircut.

And that is the friendly version. If your shares are RSUs that vest at the IPO, they get taxed as ordinary income. Now you need $15.84 million of stock to buy the same house.

Industry observers note that quick note for early employees: qualified small business stock could wipe out a chunk of that federal bill. But Anthropic blew past the $50 million gross assets test years ago, so this only helps a very small number of people who got shares in 2021.

Recent findings suggest that so a $7.5 million house is worth roughly $11.9 million of Anthropic stock today. I set the line at $8.5 million because the stock also gets four years to grow, and the house does not grow nearly as fast.

I have a long-standing belief that equity in a firm is a type of funny money. The value is based on growth and profit assumptions years into the future. A stock provides no utility. Its value can tank overnight, like we've seen with NVIDIA and many tech stocks recently. You can look at it on a screen, but that's about it.

In a recent development, only when you sell it and buy something does it become real. And the moment you sell it, the government takes a third or more.

According to recent reports, A house is different. A house pays you every single day in the form of shelter you do not have to rent. Your goal in getting rich from stock is to buy the dream house, not the other way around.

It has been revealed that owning that $7.5 million home outright costs $117,750 a year, and property taxes are almost the whole story at $87,750. Utilities, gardening, and services run $15,000. Maintenance on a freshly remodeled house is about $10,000. Insurance is $5,000. So “free and clear” still costs you $9,812 a month before you buy a single grocery.

In a recent development, but renting the same house in San Francisco costs about $25,000 a month, a 4% gross yield. So owning it beats renting it by $182,250 a year, and that gap grows. Over the six-month lockup alone, that is $91,125 handed to a landlord while you wait for permission to sell.

Proposition 13. Your assessment is locked at your purchase price and can only rise 2% a year. If the house doubles, your tax bill does not. Meanwhile your stock's tax bill grows right alongside the gain.

In a recent development, the $500,000 exclusion. A married couple shields half a million of gain when they sell a primary residence. Anthropic stock gets zero exclusion.

According to recent reports, you can borrow against it without triggering a taxable event. Try getting a line of credit against locked-up pre-IPO shares.

Sources indicate that and there is the part that does not show up in a spreadsheet. Your kids get bedrooms. You might get a rare enclosed front yard, or the sunset ocean view at 7pm. You cannot raise a family inside a brokerage account.

Now let me argue against myself, because the bull case is not stupid.

Anthropic's 2026 annualized revenue run rate is about $80 billion, up from roughly $47 billion in May and about $9 billion at the end of 2025. The organization also reported its first positive adjusted operating income, reversing a loss of about $5.6 billion in 2024.

Here is my pro forma, and I am deliberately staying inside the firm's own guidance. I have the run rate at $90 billion by December 2026, $150 billion by December 2027, and $200 billion by December 2028. Growth decelerates from 67% to 33%, which is still extraordinary for a business of that size.

If those numbers land, which I think they will because companies sandbag their first guidance, the multiple does the work for you. Whatever Anthropic prices at, that number gets cut roughly in half by the end of 2027 and in half again by the end of 2028. The organization simply grows into the price.

A house is not going to do that. A house is going to sit there and appreciate at optimistically 10% per annum, but probably closer to 5%, while asking you for a latest roof.

Say you take the $8.5 million in Anthropic stock, ride out the lockup, and blueprint to buy your dream house with an enclosed front yard in four years.

The house is not waiting for you. At 5% appreciation, $7.5 million becomes $9.1 million. And while you wait, you are renting at $25,000 a month, which burns about $1.27 million over four years.

In a recent development, so the stock has to produce $10.4 million after tax just to get you back to even. Pre-tax, that means your $8.5 million stock has to become $16.5 million. The extra $6.1 million goes to the government.

Anthropic has to appreciate 1.9 times, from wherever it prices, within four years. Call it a double. That is an 18.1% compound annual return.

If it prices at $1.4 trillion, you need $2.7 trillion. If it prices at $1.5 trillion, you need $2.9 trillion. The dollar figure moves. The requirement does not. The house costs what it costs, rent costs what it costs, and California takes what it takes. None of that cares what Goldman and Morgan Stanley settle on tonight.

A 50% gain is not enough. Up 50% leaves you with $8 million after tax, more than a million short of the asking price alone, and $2.4 million short once you count the rent you burned getting there.

If growth keeps decelerating, from 33% in 2028 to 25% in 2029 to 20% in 2030, the run rate reaches roughly $300 billion by the time the four years are up.

So the real question is what multiple of that $300 billion the market has to pay for you to break even.

Recent findings suggest that mature software companies trade at 6 to 10 times sales. Run the math across the range and there is a clean dividing line at about $1.54 trillion.

Price below that, and break-even only requires an ordinary multiple. At $1.4 trillion you need the market to pay 9.1 times sales in 2030. At $1.5 trillion, 9.7 times. Both sit inside the normal band. The stock wins even if Anthropic gets re-rated down to a perfectly boring software company.

It has been revealed that price above $1.54 trillion, and break-even requires a premium multiple that still has to be there four years from now. That is a different bet entirely, because it depends on sentiment rather than execution.

For perspective, back in September, when Anthropic was floating a $2 trillion valuation, break-even required 13 times sales.

SpaceX went public in June at around $1.75 trillion. It surged past $2 trillion, then fell back. It has been a volatile stock out of the gate, and Anthropic may trade the same way.

That is the thing about a six-month lockup. You do not get to sell into the euphoria. You get to watch it, and then you get to find out what is left when everybody else's lockup expires on the same day as yours.

The other half of this trade is that San Francisco real estate is in a melt-up, driven by the exact wealth we are discussing.

It has been revealed that between January and late June 2026, 136 single-family homes closed at or above $5 million, more than double the 67 transactions in the same period a year earlier. In June alone, 44 homes sold for at least $1 million over asking. At the very top, even all-cash offers of $25 million and up have been outbid.

This remodeled Victorian on Castro St. sold in September for $7,650,000 against a $5,495,000 list. That is 39% over asking, $2.15 million above what the sellers hoped for, for 3,416 square feet on a 2,622 square foot lot. Smaller than the house in our scenario. This is what the money actually buys here.

According to recent reports, A 4,500 square foot remodeled home on a large lot with views is a unicorn property. Homes with views usually don’t have large useable lots and vice versa. Maybe 5-8 trade in a given year. If you wait four years to buy it with your stock proceeds, you are not bidding against today's buyers. You are bidding against every other newly liquid Anthropic and OpenAI employee who made the same plan you did.

Instead of the $7.5 million house being worth $9.1 million in four years, it could be worth well north of $10 million.

That is the trap. Everybody's exit strategy is the same few houses.

It has been revealed that some of you are already typing that the answer is to take the stock and move somewhere a mansion costs $2 million. Two problems.

The job that created the windfall is in San Francisco, so leaving means leaving the equity behind. And California taxes equity compensation based on where you worked while it vested, so moving after the fact does not get you out of the bill you are trying to avoid.

Further, would you really walk away from a job like that when there are so many more millions to make? Only if you’re a FIRE person who values time and freedom more than money.

It has been revealed that as for the mansion itself, I toured a bunch of them in Honolulu last summer and came away thinking buying a mansion in paradise might be backwards. Then again, having a mansion in a beautiful city like San Francisco is a pretty amazing combination.

Real wealth is not the number. Real wealth is the gap between what you own and what you can actually enjoy.

You can spend the next four years watching a ticker and eating at home to preserve optionality, and end up with $10.4 million and four years of your kids' childhoods spent in a sub-optional rental you did not love. Or you can spend those four years in the dream house, providing for your family and making memories, and end up with $9.1 million or more of home equity plus four years you actually lived.

That remarked, I believe Anthropic could reach $3 trillion in market cap by the end of 2027 and $5 trillion by the end of 2028. Against anything in tonight's IPO price range, that is a healthy amount of upside. If I am right, the stock wins this debate within about thirteen months and it is not even a contest.

I drew the fair line myself, and I am still leaning toward the house. Watching names like Google and Nvidia drop 30% to 40% in a few months is a reminder of how fickle stocks are. And not having to fight a bidding war over a unicorn property would save my wife and me a lot of heartbreak.

It has been revealed that at 49 with two young kids, time is too precious to put my life on hold for money that won't be used. I might end up with far more money holding Anthropic stock. But by the time I sell and pay the capital gains, I doubt I can lock down the dream house at a reasonable price.

In a recent development, because if I have $20 million in Anthropic stock in four years, so do thousands of other employees and investors. Bidding against one buyer is hard enough. Bidding against dozens for the same unicorn property is impossible to win. And what good is money you cannot convert into the thing you wanted it for?

So I take the bird in hand. I have watched enough people optimize their way through a decade and arrive at the finish line wealthy and vaguely disappointed. Money is a means to an end. And one of those ends is living in the nicest house you can comfortably afford.

It has been revealed that readers, Which would you take: the $7.5 million dream house, or $8.5 million of Anthropic stock with a six-month lockup? And why? Note: All your comments eventually go through. The spam filter is just working overdrive. Thanks for your patience.

Most people reading this will not be deciding between a $7.5 million house and an IPO windfall. But the same AI boom driving both is also driving something more boring: the physical buildout underneath it. Every model needs compute, compute needs data centers, and data centers need land, power, and permits. That is real estate, and it is the constraint nobody can code their way around.

Everest and Ama Dablam Climbs Resume Despite Cyclone
