📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (567 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Getting Lost on the Camino Led to Clifftop Oasis

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today was an easy, relaxed stage mostly spent walking along the waterfront with very little elevation change.
  • According to recent reports, it turned out to be a gorgeous, sunny day with temperatures in the low 60°Fs.
  • Industry observers note that at the edge of town, an ancient fort and castle stood guard out on a rocky point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today was an easy, relaxed stage mostly spent walking along the waterfront with very little elevation change. We took our time getting started at 8:30 AM and immediately stopped at the first café we could find for some morning caffeine.

According to recent reports, it turned out to be a gorgeous, sunny day with temperatures in the low 60°Fs. While the sun felt warm on our backs, the brisk breeze blowing off the water felt like a blast of cold air conditioning.

Industry observers note that at the edge of town, an ancient fort and castle stood guard out on a rocky point. Just past the fortress, the road narrowed and hugged a dramatic path carved directly into a cliffside above the pounding ocean. Both of us were completely in awe of the scenery.

Fortunately, a wide pedestrian walkway separated us from the rush of passing cars. We followed this coastal stretch until reaching the next town, where the trail finally turned inland.

According to recent reports, once we headed inland, the path climbed into the hills—and we rapidly got lost once again. After some backtracking, we found our way back onto the official Camino route and continued our ascent.

In a recent development, we followed narrow residential streets steadily uphill until the pavement gave way to a rocky forest trail. Climbing higher through the woods, we eventually reached the crest of the hill. From the top, sweeping views of the rugged coastline stretched out both ahead and behind us, complete with a picturesque lighthouse perched on a distant point.

Sources indicate that from the ridge, we descended the forest trail until it reconnected with paved roads winding through small coastal farms. Before long, we arrived at our hotel in Mougás, perched right on a flat shelf directly above surf crashing onto the rocks below.

Industry observers note that this stretch of the coast is very rural, featuring just one small grocery store and a handful of cafés. After dropping off our packs, we grabbed a meal at a local bar, picked up a bottle of wine from the grocery store, and headed back to relax.

Our hotel featured a pool area with a large grassy lawn right on the edge of the cliffs overlooking the ocean. The sun was shining brightly enough for us to shed our extra layers and soak up the afternoon warmth—a truly perfect ending to a very chill day on the Camino.

Latest Update: Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • It has been revealed that “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

It has been revealed that “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

On a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

According to recent reports, “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

Vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

In a recent development, baia indicates the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

On Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no newly introduced soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Sources indicate that yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

The Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

Tech Report: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing fresh route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • In the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing fresh route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

In the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin mentioned. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

It has been revealed that bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” remarked Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

In a recent development, for Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he said.

According to recent reports, there are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

In a recent development, if your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

In a recent development, once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson remarked. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” mentioned Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

That stated, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

Sources indicate that buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the major cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

In a recent development, to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

It has been revealed that ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

Sources indicate that conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Recent findings suggest that marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin remarked.

It has been revealed that “That is why it is notable to consider all options and potential challenges before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they noted. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

They warn that conditions in the Andes are changing swiftly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

It has been revealed that sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he mentioned.

It has been revealed that the climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they said.

Breaking: Roads Less Traveled

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I explore some alternative routes through the mountains to finish my hike in Pennsylvania.
  • As predicted, I was all set on sleep around 5:00AM.
  • It has been revealed that it didn’t take long to notice that my left leg was feeling a little goofy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I explore some alternative routes through the mountains to finish my hike in Pennsylvania. One works out well while the other does not.

As predicted, I was all set on sleep around 5:00AM. Less predictable was the state of my left hip, which I had been sleeping on throughout most of the night and which was experiencing some discomfort. Counterintuitively, my “good” night of sleep with less waking during the night meant I spent too much time sleeping on one side of my body. Normally I wake up a handful of times and roll around to change my sleeping position. Time would tell if that would spill over into my hike. I opened my tent to hang up my water filter to get some water ready for breakfast and noticed that my interior mesh was ever so slightly damp. Indeed, the inside of my rain fly was wet. It hadn’t rained, I figured we must have had an unusually humid night. Not ideal. I was determined to get an early start on the day, I managed to have breakfast in my tent and get packing underway before sunrise. I scrambled onto Table Rock to watch the sun rise over Third Mountain. It was somewhere in the mid 30s this morning, with the humidity the cold was piercing through my shoulder-season apparel like it was barely there. Movement is the best cure so after snapping a few pictures of the sunrise I headed back to my tent, finished packing, and at 7:15AM was heading north on the trail eager to move Pennsylvania into the “Done” column.

It has been revealed that it didn’t take long to notice that my left leg was feeling a little goofy. There was a sensation in my hip that made me feel like I was stepping too narrow. I try swinging my leg around to loosen it up, but it didn’t help. My only choice was to hope it would go away once I warmed up.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

A darn good spot to camp for the night if I say so myself.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

Industry observers note that last evening I studied the topographic map on FarOut and found that the gravel road between Second and Third Mountain is a viable alternative route back to my van. It would be roughly the same distance as the AT, but flatter and with less rocks, assuming gravel doesn’t count as rocks. I love a good alternate route that let’s me get a different perspective on my return leg so it felt like a no-brainer.

The day began to slowly warm up as I hiked along Peters Mountain. By the time I was descending back into the valley the sun was shining directly on the south side of the ridge and providing plenty of warmth. Ahead was the climb up Third Mountain, knowing that I was about to get warm awfully I fast I stopped to shed my sleeping layers and load them into my pack. To connect to the gravel road, I needed to take the Knauber Trail up Third Mountain. It proved a tough, direct route up the mountain. The trail didn’t seem to get nearly as many visitors as the AT. There were leaves piled up several inches thick and I was having to heave myself up the trail with my trekking poles since my shoes were prone to slipping. I arrived at the crest of the ridge in a huff, and promptly felt the temperature drop now that I was between mountain ridges, out of the sun, and no longer climbing. My gloves went back on, and I decided to tough it out in my single layer sun hoodie rather than dig out my other layers.

Sunlight beams onto the trail toward Third Mountain.

Turning off onto the Knauber Trail.

The Knauber Trail proves to be a steep, leafy challenge.

Recent findings suggest that the gravel road passed through a mountain gap and descended into the Stony Creek Valley. On the way, I passed an upright stone marker noting the spot where members of the Kabob Hiking Club have been gathering annually to commemorate the founding of their club. Apparently it began in 1934. This location is well off the beaten track. I suppose you could drive down the gravel road easily enough, but be prepared for a long drive.

Industry observers note that once the road settled between Second and Third Mountain it followed Stony Creek for what I imagine is somewhere between 8 and 10 miles. There are stretches of the road where you can see a full mile ahead, maybe more. It was honestly a little unsettling. Imagine hiking 10 minutes and the view ahead hardly looks any different. I found it more comforting to focus on the ground below me, at least that was moving. I enjoyed the steady progress, though there wasn’t much to see or report on, just pine trees and not a soul to be found.

The gravel road descends sharply to the Stony Creek Valley.

Yeesh that is a long, straight road.

Once I had made my way down the gravel road I took a moment to visit a few other markers at Rausch Creek. One sign explained the structures next to the creek were indeed filters as I had guessed yesterday. They use limestone to clean the water, which is why it looked so clear. I suspect the light gray color of the limestone settling on the bottom of the creek also helps the water to look brighter and more clear than if the creek bed were covered in natural rock.

As I made my way back toward Second Mountain I passed back through a flat section of trail that seems to flood regularly. Beavers had dammed some of the creeks and the soft soil caused many of the trees to fall, creating a relatively open area. Oddly, a plaid shirt was hung in the middle of the bog, one can only assume it belonged to one of the beaver’s victims.

Sources indicate that with one final push I made my way up to Second Mountain where I made a miscalculation. High on the success of my gravel road alternate route, I decided to double down and take what appeared to be a shortcut. The AT crosses an abandoned dirt road which seemed to lead back toward the road not far from the trailhead where my van was parked. I found it odd that the road bent at a 90 degree angle just ahead on the map, but thought little of it. I forged along the road and did see a turn, but it was slightly too early to be the 90 degree turn on the map. Continuing on, the road continued straight ahead, which wasn’t shown on the map. There was also no 90 degree turn where it should have been. I decided to stick with the road that I was on even though I didn’t know exactly where it would go. Really, there were only two options, it would either end up near the road I was looking for, or it would turn a bit and eventually rejoin the AT.

It turned out to be the latter, albeit after some unwelcome elevation gain that meant I probably lost a bit of time by taking this route. My hip, which had gotten better after the first mile or so, acted up again around mile 20. It is a good thing I have a day off tomorrow for it to bounce back. It was nearly 4:00PM when I was back on the road making my way back to my van. I decided to use the afternoon to drive down to Hagerstown, Maryland so I could spend all day tomorrow focusing on tying up any remaining loose ends before starting off on my final section of the trail.

Entering the bog between Second and Third Mountains.

This is all that remains of the last hiker to trifled with the beavers.

Passing back through the meadow near Swatara Gap.

Total: 23.6 miles, 50,859 steps.

To learn more, please visit the About This Site page.

Industry observers note that I’m See You Tomorrow (SYT), a 30-something hiker who loves hiking just for the thrill of seeing things that most people don’t. I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am newly introduced to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!

Once again, thank you for the sunrise photos. Beautiful! You’re very blessed I’m sure you’re done by now. Can’t wait to read your last post and I know you’re doing a trail out west next year. I’ll be looking forward to that. See you tomorrow.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
  • Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • In a recent development, according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

In a recent development, according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

According to recent reports, the following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

It has been revealed that “He was really lucky,” said Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

It has been revealed that by the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

#113828. Weekend Warm-Up: Behind the Climb

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Weekend Warm-Up: Behind the Climb

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (426 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
  • As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • The Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

The Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

Interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

It has been revealed that ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed plan.

Sources indicate that despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

At the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

#113825. Industry News: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1709 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Recent findings suggest that gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • Sources indicate that the journey has not gone according to blueprint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Recent findings suggest that gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

Sources indicate that the journey has not gone according to blueprint. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

In a recent development, given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid aims. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Industry observers note that roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

Recent findings suggest that for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Recent findings suggest that northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and initiative ahead.

In a recent development, the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line demonstrates the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

According to recent reports, I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

Recent findings suggest that I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Recent findings suggest that food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Industry observers note that safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

The kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

Recent findings suggest that we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

It has been revealed that successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

Recent findings suggest that I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

You have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

Sources indicate that we were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

Industry observers note that there is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

Sources indicate that I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

It has been revealed that university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

Recent findings suggest that the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

The actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

You can follow the expedition here.

No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (391 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • Recent findings suggest that “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • According to recent reports, in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is swiftly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

Recent findings suggest that “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

According to recent reports, in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

It has been revealed that on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

According to recent reports, once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

#113820. The 2026 Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey: General Information (Part 1)

The 2026 Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey: General Information (Part 1)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Each year, The Trek asks all Appalachian Trail hikers to complete a survey about their hike preparation, trail experiences, and personal backpacking journeys.
  • According to recent reports, our hope is that this survey serves as a great resource for prospective Appalachian Trail thru-hikers as they initiative and prepare for their hike.
  • A note on the data: As this survey is intended to help prospective thru-hikers strategy for the trail, we filter the responses to only include those who either initially planned to complete the entire trail or those who hiked enough on the trail to have pertinent statistics to thru-hikers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Each year, The Trek asks all Appalachian Trail hikers to complete a survey about their hike preparation, trail experiences, and personal backpacking journeys. We’ve taken all the information from our 293 responses this year and have analyzed it to help you better understand the Appalachian Trail Class of 2026.

According to recent reports, our hope is that this survey serves as a great resource for prospective Appalachian Trail thru-hikers as they initiative and prepare for their hike. However, please keep in mind that no two hikes look the same, and you should by no means feel obligated to follow the trends or “averages” presented here. Use this data as a guide to inform your decisions, but remember that the most successful hike is the one that works best for you.

A note on the data: As this survey is intended to help prospective thru-hikers strategy for the trail, we filter the responses to only include those who either initially planned to complete the entire trail or those who hiked enough on the trail to have pertinent statistics to thru-hikers.

We therefore excluded responses from hikers who hiked less than 500 miles and never intended to thru-hike; those who intended to complete an AT thru-hike but needed to stop before hiking 500 miles are still included. If you have any feedback on this benchmark, please leave a comment and let us know what you think the cutoff should be for 2027.

Using this framework, we have collected data from 294 AT long-distance hikers in 2026. The number will rise as we continue to accept responses from southbound hikers, and this survey will be updated with their information later into 2027.

This first post will focus on the broader demographics and logistics for Appalachian Trail hikers, while the next post will dig into the on-trail experiences and favorites/least favorites of this year’s Class.

AT Thru-Hiker Demographics Prior Experience, Injuries, and Completion Rates Direction, Start and Finish Dates, and Pace Budget.

The age distribution of hikers starting the trail remains generally consistent year over year, though 2026 pushed the upper boundaries of the age range even further. This season, our youngest hiker was 16 years old, while at the other end of the spectrum, the oldest hiker was 76. (For comparison, the 2025 range spanned from 12 to 73, and 2024 ran from 18 to 71.).

Notably, though he did not fill out our survey, Dale “Grey Beard” Sanders was the oldest thru-hiker on trail this year, setting the age record for an Appalachian Trail thru-hike at 91.

It has been revealed that we continue to see a large core group of hikers in their 20s and early 30s. These are typically recent college graduates and those unburdened by mortgage or family ties. This group is followed by another notable wave of hikers in their late 50s and early 60s, as retirees use their extra time and financial stability to take on the trail.

Sources indicate that this year, the average age of an AT thru-hiker was 39, which remains much higher than the most commonly reported age of 25. In statistics, when the mean (39) sits well above the median (34) and mode (25), it points to a long tail end of older participants pulling the overall average upward.

READ NEXT: The Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey: All Years.

Recent findings suggest that since The Trek began collecting demographic data for the survey in 2016, the gender distribution has fluctuated between around 54 and 63% men. In 2025, 63% of survey respondents were men, which was the highest proportion of men to date.

This year, we stay consistent with that high proportion of men at 62.5%, while responses from women rose slightly to 34.8% and non-binary respondents held steady at just over 2%.

The trail remains overwhelmingly (96%) White, a trend that persists year over year as the proportion of White respondents has consistently landed above 90% since we began collecting demographic data in 2016.

While efforts to diversify the outdoors continue, the demographic data highlights that hikers identifying as White still make up the overwhelming majority, with fewer than 4% of hikers identifying as Hispanic, Asian, Black, Native American, or Pacific Islander. This number, while already small, is even smaller than in 2025, when we saw just over 4% of hikers identifying as non-White.

Sources indicate that as with previous years, the vast majority of survey respondents in 2026 (90%) were from the United States. Eleven other countries were represented among the respondents, which is slightly more than we saw last year, with international hikers primarily coming from Canada, the UK, and Germany.

Within the United States, the majority of hikers continued to hail from eastern and Mid-Atlantic states, taking advantage of closer geographic proximity to the trail.

Recent findings suggest that as in previous years, we hypothesize that hikers from eastern states are more likely to tackle the AT due to easier travel logistics and greater familiarity and emotional connection with the area. Last year, Colorado marked the non-eastern state with the most respondents; this year, only 6 responses came from Colorado while Ohio and Texas each produced 10.

The states producing the most respondents this year were North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Virginia, tied for the top spot with 21 respondents each and closely followed by Georgia at 15 — all states found along the Appalachian Trail.

Education levels remained consistent with previous years — our survey indicates that Appalachian Trail thru-hikers continue to be a highly educated group, with two-thirds of respondents holding a Bachelor’s, graduate, or professional degree.

Similar to prior years, the small fraction of respondents indicating they did not finish high school is largely (though not entirely) accounted for by younger hikers who took on the trail as recent graduates or during gap periods.

Industry observers note that this year, respondents hailed from over 200 distinct occupations before starting the trail. We’ve grouped them into the above categories, with STEM & Professional Services (Engineering, Technology, Science, Finance, Law, and Corporate Administration) once again leading the pack at 35.4% of responses.

In a recent development, students and educators continue to make up a significant segment of the thru-hiking community. Educators alone account for 5.5% of respondents. When we asked participants how they secured the time off to thru-hike, 7.3% of respondents cited having summers off or seasonal flexibility, while another 6.9% leveraged scheduled breaks from school.

As in prior years, nearly 38.1% of respondents quit their jobs entirely to hike. Combined with the 23.2% who are retired, career breaks, transitions, and retirement make up over 60% of the total AT Class of 2026, showing how much a long-distance trail can stem from or cause a major life pivot.

Industry observers note that the average hiker on the Appalachian Trail in 2026 had between one and seven nights of prior backpacking experience, with nearly 30% of respondents falling into the 1-to-3-nights bracket and over 21% falling into the 4-to-7-nights range. Very few respondents reported having no prior hiking or backpacking experience at all. Meanwhile, a strong group (13.3%) reported 3 months or more of prior experience, likely representing hikers who had previously completed other long-distance trails.

According to recent reports, this year, we also examined the rates of unplanned early exits from trail across these prior experience levels. Interestingly, the data demonstrates that prior backpacking experience does not strictly dictate success; hikers with modest experience (such as 1-3 nights or 4-7 nights) experienced relatively stable and moderate rates of not finishing (23% and 23.4%, respectively).

Those with zero prior backpacking experience did face a higher-than-average attrition rate (31.6% for day hikers only and 50% for the two hikers who reported never hiking or camping, for what that tiny dataset is worth). Overall, though, the data continues to corroborate the idea that the Appalachian Trail can successfully be a first major thru-hike for well-prepared beginners.

This year, 73.9% of survey respondents completed thru-hikes with over 2,000 miles hiked, rebounding nicely from last year’s rate of 63.7% and surpassing the 71% mark reported in 2024.

However, this continues to trend much higher than the completion rates reported by the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC), which historically hovers around a 25% to 30% success rate. There are a few key reasons for this consistent disparity.

Recent findings suggest that first, the ATC captures a massive dataset of every registered start, whereas our survey relies on voluntary responses. Second, because we promote our survey through The Trek and our Instagram and community channels, we naturally attract responses from hikers who are plugged into the thru-hiking ecosystem and are often better equipped and more motivated to finish.

We speculate that readers of The Trek are simply better prepared for the physical and mental demands of the trail after engaging with our guides and community. While we can’t prove that our content is the secret sauce to a successful AT thru-hike, please let us keep believing it for the sake of our ego.

75 survey respondents this year did not complete a full thru-hike. Of that group, 13.3% (10 hikers) stated they only intended to hike a section or had already reached their personal mileage goal. That represents a sharp decline from 2025, when planned section hikers accounted for 39% of the non-finishing respondents (likely because we worked harder to filter out short-distance section hikers from the dataset this year).

It has been revealed that when we look at the 65 hikers who experienced an unplanned exit from the trail, injury remains the undisputed primary reason, accounting for 38.7% of all non-finishers. Tying for the next most common reasons were family/personal obligations and mental burnout (such as boredom or loss of motivation), each accounting for 13.3% of respondents who left the trail.

Interestingly, while 2025 was an anomaly where zero respondents cited finances as their reason for leaving the trail, money troubles returned in 2026: running out of funds accounted for 8% of exits (6 hikers), tying with illness and the general physical toll of the trail.

Sources indicate that one important note about this data: though we advertise this survey to the best of our ability, many hikers who unexpectedly left the trail early are likely not engaging with Appalachian Trail media by the time autumn rolls around. As a result, our responses remain skewed toward those who completed their hikes as planned, meaning we are likely only seeing a partial picture of trail attrition.

Not only were injuries the largest cause of needing to leave the trail, but they were also quite pervasive among all the hikers on trail. More than half of our survey respondents (55.4%) experienced an injury during their 2026 hike, while 44.6% made it through unscathed.

Getting hurt on the Appalachian Trail does not automatically mean the end of the trail. Over 81% of injured hikers managed to stay on the trail by adapting their routine. Nearly a third of those injured (32.5%) hiked through the pain without taking any time off. Another 28.1% dialed back their daily mileage to recover, while 20.6% took some time off the trail.

Ultimately, 18.8% of reported injuries were hike-ending (9.9% of all respondents).

In 2026, hike direction returned to its traditional pre-Hurricane Helene baseline, with the proportion of Northbound hikers jumping nearly 13 percentage points to 92.9% (up from 80.2% in 2025). Conversely, Flip-Flop hikes dropped from 13.5% to 5.0%, and Southbound respondents fell from 6.3% to 2.1%.

According to recent reports, that shift confirms last year’s spike in alternative itineraries was largely a temporary response to Hurricane Helene. Ahead of the 2025 season, the ATC and media outlets (like us!) encouraged hikers to pursue Southbound or Flip-Flop hikes to give southern trail towns and trail crews time to rebuild. With the southern portion of the trail recovered and reopened for the 2026 season, the vast majority of thru-hikers returned to the classic Georgia-to-Maine route.

Despite expectations last year that Southbound numbers would continue to climb as more people learned about the benefits of hiking south, the pull of the traditional Northbound social bubble remains hard to beat.

Most hikers began their hikes in March and April (accounting for nearly 75% of all start dates), with the single most popular start date this year shifting about two weeks earlier to March 14, closely followed by March 9.

In a recent development, we asked respondents if they were satisfied with their start dates, and satisfaction jumped even higher this year: 94% of all respondents reported being happy with when they set out. Because the 2026 bubble shifted slightly earlier into March, the average start date for satisfied NOBO hikers moved up to March 18 (compared to March 29 in 2025).

Meanwhile, the average start date for NOBO hikers who felt they started too early was February 12, while the average date for those who felt they started too late fell between April 8 and April 10. With over 9 out of 10 hikers satisfied with their choice, the “right” start date ultimately comes down to the type of trail experience you want to have.

Industry observers note that the small handful of hikers who felt they started too late cited weather concerns, wanting a slower pace during the first few weeks, not having enough time to heal from an injury and still finish, or feeling stressed as a solo hiker at the tail end of the bubble. Conversely, the five hikers who felt they started too early pointed to cold winter weather in February and early March. One April 6 starter noted they actually wished the trail had been more crowded.

If you want to start in what most thru-hikers consider the “sweet spot” for Northbounders, aim for a mid-to-late March window, keeping in mind that starting right in the March bubble means sharing shelters and campsites with bigger crowds early on.

Recent findings suggest that southbound hikers start later in the season — this year ranging from May 29 to August 12, with most setting out in late May and June — to let winter conditions clear up north. All eight of our current Southbound respondents reported being satisfied with their start dates, though the sample size remains too small to track broader date trends.

This year we’re keeping the survey open for Southbound applicants who are still on trail, and we’ll be back with more SOBO data early in 2027. SOBOs: click here to take the 2026 Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey.

According to recent reports, most successful thru-hikers finish between mid-July and mid-October, with September (86 hikers) and August (65 hikers) as the peak months for summiting Katahdin. The single most popular finish date this year was September 15 (9 hikers), closely followed by September 19 and August 26.

While a small handful of fast-moving Northbounders finished as early as late May and June — led by one early starter who wrapped up on May 31 and noted it was too early for weather-related reasons — the vast majority timed their finishes for late summer and early autumn, well within Baxter State Park’s typical May-to-October operating window.

Sources indicate that overall, 94.4% of thru-hikers reported being satisfied with their finish date. The average finish date that Northbound hikers were satisfied with was August 27 (shifting a little over two weeks later than last year’s August 11 average), while the average finish date reported as too late for weather-related reasons was September 10 for Northbounders. Two Northbound hikers who summited on September 19 and September 20 felt their finish dates were too crowded, landing right in the heart of the mid-September summit bubble.

In a recent development, with the information on start and end dates, we can look at the duration and pacing of hikers’ treks. We filtered this data to only include respondents who completed a thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail.

In a recent development, the average completed thru-hike this year took 160 days (just over five months), ticking up slightly from last year’s 153-day average. The longest reported thru-hike was 230 days (a flip-flopper who started February 27 and finished October 12), while the fastest completed thru-hike was an 88-day Southbound trek, followed closely by two Northbounders who finished in 96 days.

Sources indicate that we also asked self-reported thru-hikers about their average daily mileage, with the overall average across respondents coming in at 15.0 miles per day (up from 14.3 miles per day in 2025). The single most-reported daily mileage was once again 15 miles per day (31 hikers), followed closely by 14 and 13 miles per day.

Even though our survey asks hikers to include zero days in their estimate, many respondents likely reported their hiking-day average rather than their true calendar average, or simply guessed without tracking exact daily numbers. Treat this figure as a loose ballpark: at the trail’s official length of 2,197.9 miles, the average 160-day thru-hike works out to a true calendar pace of roughly 13.7 miles per day once zero days and town stops are factored in.

It has been revealed that attendance at trail festivals rebounded strongly in 2026, driven by a return to classic Northbound traffic and high engagement among thru-hikers. While 44.2% of survey respondents still reported not attending any trail festival, that figure dropped significantly from 2025 (when 56% reported no festival attendance) as crowds returned to trail towns.

Trail Days in Damascus, Virginia remains by far the most popular AT festival, with 44.2% of respondents attending. Meanwhile, the Northbound Kickoff at Amicalola Falls saw a significant attendance bump, drawing 11.6% of respondents.

Unlike in prior years, we filtered our financial questions to include only those who completed their thru-hikes, to better reflect how much it actually costs to hike the entire trail.

Likely in part due to this decision, the average cost of an Appalachian Trail thru-hike (including the cost of gear) climbed notably this year to $8,863 (compared to $7,680 in 2025 and $7,602 in 2024), with a median spend of $8,500 and many hikers reporting total costs exceeding $10,000.

The spread of hikers across the cost spectrum reveals significant spikes around $6,000 and $8,000, along with 28 hikers reporting spending $10,000. At the extreme ends, only 6 hikers reported spending under $2,500, while 15 reported spending $15,000 or more.

Hikers spent an average of $2,305 on their gear in 2026 across all respondents who completed 500 miles or more on the AT, ticking up moderately from previous years. The median gear spend was $2,000, with the most common spending bracket also at $2,000 (57 hikers).

The vast majority of hikers spent under $4,000 on their gear, which covers the initial cost of purchasing packs, tents, and sleep systems along with the ongoing replacement or repair of footwear, clothing, and worn-out items over the course of their journey.

While most kept their setups budget-friendly or mid-tier with their spend peaking between $1,000 and $2,500, a few outliers scaled the high end of the luxury spectrum, with 11 respondents reporting gear investments exceeding $10,000 (including two hikers topping out at $11,000).

Sources indicate that to those few hikers who absolutely splurged, shoot me a message. I’d love to know what on earth is in your pack.

We’re stopping here for now, but there is plenty more data to come. In the next few posts, we will break down everything from hiker experience levels and safety concerns to the nitty-gritty gear stats on shelters, footwear, and backpacks.

Looking for other years? Find every Trek AT thru-hiker survey on our Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey page.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • Industry observers note that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

Industry observers note that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He noted climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants to build a new military base, and some public land states like Wyoming say they have just the spots.
  • The base would house between 15,000 and 25,000 active-duty service members, according to a red, white and blue competition flier for what Hegseth is calling the Next Great American Base contest.
  • It has been revealed that hegseth stated the base should be a “dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform” with its own power generation, modern air defenses, and advanced technology, reported Newsweek in early October, when the call for pitches first arrived.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants to build a new military base, and some public land states like Wyoming say they have just the spots.

The base would house between 15,000 and 25,000 active-duty service members, according to a red, white and blue competition flier for what Hegseth is calling the Next Great American Base contest. And ideally it would include 100,000 to 250,000 contiguous acres.

It has been revealed that hegseth stated the base should be a “dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform” with its own power generation, modern air defenses, and advanced technology, reported Newsweek in early October, when the call for pitches first arrived. He went on to say the best proposals would cut through “the red tape, offering up the land and rolling out the red carpet for our military families.”.

According to recent reports, but much of the “red tape” associated with building a base on hundreds of thousands of acres of unoccupied land is likely federal government red tape. And no clear path currently exists for how to requisition and build a latest military installation on federal public land, remarked Mark Squillace, a natural resources law professor at the University of Colorado Law School.

Sources indicate that the Department of Defense would need to work around current Bureau of Land Management or U.S. Forest Service management looks that include stipulations for wildlife like migration corridors and winter range closures.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also unclear if the base needs to support the U.S. Navy, which would limit public-land options since the bulk of the country’s public lands are in the Interior West like Nevada, Idaho and Utah, though the fact sheet claims all locations, even those without water access, are on the table.

The DOD already administers 8.4 million acres in the U.S., but is looking to acquire lands managed by other agencies.

In a recent development, wyoming, for its part, is eyeing both state and federal land for the base. The state’s adjutant general, Maj. Gen. Greg Porter, told a legislative committee in early November that Wyoming has identified at least four “chunks” of state and federal land, as reported by the Cowboy State Daily last week. Which chunks have not yet been disclosed.

Squillace lined out how building a military base on public land could — or could not — become a reality.

Sources indicate that the DOD would first likely need to discuss any public land acquisition with the BLM or Forest Service. If the land use agency agrees that a military base would fit the current land management strategy, it would need to prepare a draft Environmental Impact Statement that brings up potential complications and confirms compliance with laws like the Endangered Species Act or National Historic Preservation Act.

Industry observers note that “A positive review would likely lead to temporary withdrawal of the land from the operation of certain public land laws (like mining and leasing) that could interfere with the operation of the base,” Squillace says, while also noting that existing rights would be protected. Any particularly valuable mining claims would have to be bought out in what he describes as a “time consuming and expensive” process.

Read Next: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

Ultimately, however, Squillace claims any large-scale, long-term use of land would likely need to be approved by Congress, “since such transfers of public land are not authorized under law.”  Whether or not the dramatically different Congress to be sworn in next year would green light a public-land transfer requested by Hegseth also remains uncertain.

  • Miltroka found a likely spot and, well before daybreak on Monday, he was in a tree saddle with his Ruger American Generation II chambered in 7mm PRC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, indiana’s state park system offers a limited draw hunt that allows residents to target the abundant whitetails on park land that doesn’t get much hunting pressure. There are about 25 parks in the popular program, with two firearms hunts allowed on most of them. Each hunt runs just two days.

It has been revealed that “I put in for the early two-day hunt on November 16 and 17 at a Northeast Indiana state park and got drawn for it,” Mike Miltroka tells Outdoor Life. “Trail cameras are not allowed on park [land]. But you can scout before hunt days. I scouted the park on Sunday, the day before the first day of hunting on November 16.”.

Miltroka found a likely spot and, well before daybreak on Monday, he was in a tree saddle with his Ruger American Generation II chambered in 7mm PRC.

Recent findings suggest that “It was cool and a little windy, but I was seeing deer soon after daybreak,” says Miltroka, a 38-year-old long-haul truck driver from Farmland. “I spotted a good buck far out, but the cover was too thick to shoot.”.

It has been revealed that as the morning wore on, Miltroka got a chance to take two does, and he dropped them both with his Ruger. He toted both does to his truck using a deer cart, since motorized vehicles are not allowed off-road.

The spot was already paying off, and Miltroka had a friend — who had seen a giant deer using the area before the hunt — to thank for tipping him off about it.

“I’d never seen the deer previously, but a buddy showed me a video [he’d taken] of the buck a month earlier while visiting the park … It was a place no one else was hunting, and I checked to make sure it was okay to hunt there – and it was.”.

On the second day of the hunt, Miltroka chose a different tree. He climbed into a major walnut closer to the cover where he’d seen the buck on Monday. But unlike the day before, Miltroka didn’t see much except a coyote. Then, around 8:30, things changed.

“I heard something raking trees behind me, and I didn’t know what it was. I kept trying to see what was making all that racket, then I saw him out about 70 yards,” he says. “I knew it was a good shooter buck, and when I got him in my scope I squeezed the trigger, fired, and the deer took off running.”.

Miltroka jacked another round into the chamber, but as soon as he picked up the running buck in his scope again, the deer went down.

It wasn’t until Miltroka studied the dead buck through his scope that he realized how immense the deer was.

Sources indicate that “I started shaking, and yelling,” he says. “I got buck fever after it was over … I called a friend of mine and was so excited he asked if I was tied tight to my tree, and I said yes. I was shaking so much I might have fallen out of it.”.

Once he was steady enough, Miltroka climbed down and walked up on the deer.

In a recent development, “I was in complete shock,” he states. “I’ve only taken about six bucks, and none even have the size of this one. I was screaming with joy.”.

Industry observers note that he filled out a transport tag for his buck, which filled his limit of three deer for the park hunt – only one of which can be a buck. Then he wheeled the buck to his vehicle, loaded it, and drove to park headquarters to check it in.

The buck’s field dressed weight was 181 pounds. The 22-point nontypical was green scored by an official Boone & Crockett measurer the day after Miltroka shot it. It gross scored 227 inches, with a net score of 197 6/8s inches. It has an outside antler spread of nearly 25 inches, and one main beam of the rack measures over 27 inches.

Recent findings suggest that he will have the buck scored again after the required 60-day drying period for B&C and will enter the buck into B&C’s nontypical record category. He’ll also submit his buck to the Hoosier Record Buck Program.

In a recent development, “The park hunts are well run and there are plenty of deer,” says Miltroka. “I saw lots of deer being checked in during the hunts and some nice bucks.

“I’m stunned at the size of my deer. But there are so many great bucks that have come from Indiana.”.

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

According to recent reports, the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

In a recent development, the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

On their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.
