📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Cold as Death,” appeared in the October 1955 issue of Outdoor Life.

There has never been anything along the upper Mississippi, before or since, like the Armistice Day storm of 1940.

It started out as a mild, cloudy morning with the temperature between 50 and 60. Fellows went duck hunting in shirt sleeves. The wind picked up velocity as the day went along, but not enough to get excited about — not until late afternoon. Then, with little warning, a full-scale prairie blizzard screamed in out of the northwest.

Industry observers note that by dark the air was smoking with gale-driven snow, and the thermometer plunged near zero. Bitter winds blew all night. The weather experts said afterward that gusts hit 80 miles an hour. The storm laid a track of death and destruction across six states; it pounded ships to pieces on the Great Lakes, blocked roads, isolated towns, paralyzed cities, and buried cars. Hundreds were marooned on highways. A crack streamliner was 27 hours late into Minneapolis. And when the morning of November 12 broke, 20 duck hunters lay dead, frozen in stiff, grotesque poses — scattered on mud bars, sand spits, and willow-grown islands of the Mississippi bottoms between Red Wing, Minnesota, and La Crosse, Wisconsin.

I was among the luckier ones. I spent that terrible night with two companions under an overturned skiff on a mud bar — wet from head to foot, without fire or heavy clothing, pants frozen to my legs, and kept alive only by the body warmth of the men who lay huddled on both sides of me. The storm cost me six weeks of agony in a hospital and half of my left foot. But at least I survived.

I was 14 at the time, attending high school in my home town of Winona, Minnesota. We got out of classes at 11 o’clock because it was Armistice Day. I scurried for home, planning an afternoon of duck hunting.

It has been revealed that the wind was already fairly fresh and mother was uneasy. “The storm warnings are up,” she told me while getting my lunch. But I grew up in Winona and knew the river, and at that age, bad weather didn’t worry me. The only thing it meant to me was good shooting. Ducks had been scarce all fall and maybe a blow would bring ’em down. So I hurried through lunch, impatient to get in a blind.

While I was loading my gear in the car, my cousin, Bob Stephens, revealed up with a partner, Cal Wieczorek, and they decided to join me. Bob was 20, Cal about 19.

We drove to the Prairie Island spillway at the lower end of the Winona pool, where Dad kept his boat. It was a 16-footer, pointed at both ends, with a homemade bracket for an outboard. We decided to hunt a place known as the Firing Line, along the border of the Upper Mississippi Wildlife Refuge, three or four miles upstream. Hunters lined up there to intercept ducks flying in and out of the refuge. In stormy weather the pass-shooting was exceptionally good, and this looked like that kind of day.

Sources indicate that the wind was blowing half a gale now and was beginning to bite. Ominous dark clouds raced overhead, and scuds of cold rain pelted down as we clamped our old three-horse outboard on the boat, cranked it up, and headed out into the choppy pool. The three of us were a heavy load, and the skiff made slow headway against the wind.

We didn’t give it a thought then, but we couldn’t have been more poorly prepared. I was wearing cotton clothes — pants, shirt, socks, and a jacket lighter than a hunting coat. I had overshoes over my leather shoes. Bob and Cal were dressed similarly, except for hip boots. Cal and I had gloves. Bob had a heavy raincoat, and I still believe that made the difference between living and dying for me.

We had one book of matches and no pocketknife. I was carrying a 16 gauge single-barrel Winchester; the other two had pumps. Because we intended to pass-shoot, we took no decoys.

Backed up by a series of low dams, the Mississippi is two to three miles wide in that section, flooding its bottoms and forming open lakes, meandering channels, small islands, bars, and rush beds. We threaded our way through this maze, wallowing in the heavy seas. It took us 1½ hours to cover the distance to the Firing Line.

Industry observers note that the sky was full of ducks; they were barreling across the bottoms in crazy skeins, riding the wind, and turning and twisting below treetop height. It was plain they didn’t like the weather. Before the afternoon was over I actually swung at a greenhead with my gun as he hovered above my head, almost stationary, while bucking the gale.

When we finally got to the Firing Line it was too crowded. The blinds were only about 25 yards apart and all occupied. Ducks were rocketing back and forth over the marsh and there was a steady barrage of shooting. We decided to find another spot.

Sources indicate that by the time we found it — on a willow-covered island with many rushes in front — we were beginning to lose interest. The wind was howling like a banshee, down off the high bluffs to the west, with sleet and fine snow in its teeth. We hunkered in the willows for almost an hour, killed four ducks, and decided we’d had enough. The cold was already bone-chilling, our hands were so stiff we could hardly handle our guns, and we were starting to worry about getting back to the landing.

It has been revealed that two strangers came by in a little duck boat; they told us they were scared. That settled it for us, but going home was easier mentioned than done. None of us knew exactly where we were, and when we tried to shove away from shore, the seas threatened to swamp us. We finally dragged the skiff to the lee side and managed to get it afloat and start the motor. But before going 200 yards we ran aground on a mud bar, which we couldn’t skirt because of the wind and seas. We dragged the boat across the bar and started on again.

Sources indicate that we did that about four times before finding ourselves by a significant open slough and admitting we were lost. It was almost dark now and snowing so hard we couldn’t see 100 feet. We couldn’t even look into the wind — the storm cut our eyeballs like a sandblast. And the slough was a welter of dirty foaming water in which our skiff probably wouldn’t last more than a minute.

While we debated what to do, another boat loomed out of the stormy dusk, riding low with four hunters. Two of them were only a little older than I — one from my home room at school. The others were men who had hunted the river bottoms all their lives. When they stated they knew the way to Prairie Island and could make it without swamping, we decided to follow.

According to recent reports, but I couldn’t get the outboard started. Bob and Cal rowed, handicapped by cold-numbed hands, while I tinkered with it. We managed to keep the other boat in sight for a few minutes. Then, pitching and rolling, it disappeared and we didn’t see it again. When our frantic yells brought no answer we realized we were again on our own. It was days before we learned what happened to the other party. Their skiff had capsized when we lost sight of it. Three of the hunters died there, standing in the icy water, not knowing which way to go to dry land. By some miracle one of the boys survived the night and rescue parties found him on a near-by island at daybreak.

Industry observers note that only a few minutes after we lost that boat we were washed ashore on a sand spit. Bob and Cal leaped clear as we grounded and escaped a wetting. I was in the stern of the skiff, working on the outboard — right in the path of a wicked sea that smashed over us the instant we touched bottom.

I can’t describe the shock that icy dunking gave me. I clawed my way out of the swamped boat, and the wind cut like a braided whip. My legs wouldn’t hold me up, so I crawled across the mud until I was beyond reach of the waves and lay there, cold and weak.

Cal and Bob dragged the boat up on dry land, turned it over, and propped one side up to make a shelter. When they finished I crawled under it. My pants and jacket crackled as I moved. They had frozen stiff in the few minutes I lay exposed to the wind.

We still had only a vague idea of our location, but we knew that large open lake, which we couldn’t cross in our puny skiff, lay between us and any landing. We didn’t talk much about it; we didn’t need to. Live or die, we’d have to spend the night where we were.

In a recent development, bob and Cal did everything possible. They gathered rushes and put them under the boat to keep me off the wet mud. Then they searched desperately for firewood, but there wasn’t so much as a scrub willow. They finally found a few pieces of water-logged driftwood, heaped them in a pyramid, and turned the outboard motor up to drain gas on it — a risky thing to do, except in a desperate emergency like ours. But the screaming wind whipped the gas into nowhere as fast as it ran out of the tank. They struck one match after another without getting a spark of fire.

The last match flared and died in the darkness, and they crawled under the boat and lay down on the wet rushes, one on each side of me. They spread their hunting coats over us and laid Bob’s raincoat on top. The raincoat kept the worst of the wind out and probably saved me from freezing.

It has been revealed that we had little sense of time and hardly talked. Bob told me afterward that I spoke only two or three times during the night, and then I worried about the anxiety my parents must be feeling.

Industry observers note that I shivered for what seemed like hours, with my hands wedged between my thighs, since that seemed to be the warmest place on my body. I prayed silently. I didn’t think much about dying. I believed we’d get through the night somehow and in the morning find our way home. I realized finally that all feeling was gone in my feet; they were wooden stumps, no longer a part of me. I must have dozed, for I recall waking up and feeling warm, but that lasted only a minute or two and then I was shivering again.

The thing I remember best was the unending scream of the wind. It never stopped raging — searching under the overturned boat, wailing, screeching, terribly alive, terribly cold.

It has been revealed that sometime in the night Bob remembered that he had two apples and two sandwiches in his hunting coat. They were frozen hard, but we gnawed at them and they seemed to help.

It has been revealed that the sound of distant gunshots reached us several times, and once we thought we heard faint, far-off yells for help. But our own guns were so crusted with ice that we couldn’t fire them, and it was useless to shout.

Industry observers note that we knew we weren’t the only hunters lost on the river bottom. Others were enduring the same torture. And we felt sure there must be rescue parties trying to find us, but we didn’t think we could count on them while the storm continued.

It was days before we learned all that happened that hard night. Rescue efforts began at dark, and men fought the storm and seas all night in skiffs and powerboats. Some even waded the sloughs to bring lost men to shore. It wasn’t a night for small craft, and no one will ever know how many boats were overturned, swamped, and driven back. But the search went on, hour after hour, heedless of the wind, cold, and snow.

According to recent reports, the night was an awful ordeal for the hunters. One party huddled on a marshy island beside a fire started with dead grass and fed with more than 40 cedar decoys. Gas from an outboard was used to rekindle the blaze each time it died down. Another group marched, jumped, and sparred around a fire built from their boats. Still another found a patch of timber, got a fire going, and then shot dead branches off trees for fuel.

Industry observers note that they were the lucky ones; others didn’t fare so well. Two died under an overturned boat, unable to see a bonfire 400 yards away. Two more reached shore along a railroad embankment, crawled halfway up the bank, fell and froze to death, too weak to walk to safety. Others gave up, lay down where they were, without fire or shelter, and died swiftly. A few drowned. Most froze. When the last of the living were rescued, the grim search for bodies continued. It was three days before all the missing were accounted for and the final toll of 20 dead was tallied.

Toward morning the air cleared enough to let me glimpse lights on the Winona dam, a few miles away. They glimmered through the driving snow, tantalizing and mocking us, but at least we knew now which direction to go when daylight came. About that same time Bob remarked that his hands were frozen and he’d probably lose them. He said it quietly, as if it didn’t really matter.

In a recent development, at first light the wind seemed to lose its gale force. It was still blowing hard, but when we studied the lake in the gray light of morning, we decided our skiff might weather the seas.

Recent findings suggest that we were in bad shape. Cal and Bob could barely stand up; I needed help to get on my feet. Our hands were stiff and useless. The spit where we spent the night was rimmed with a 50-foot belt of ice that made launching our boat a tough job. But we didn’t have much choice. We couldn’t live through the day on that bleak mud bar, and we had no way of knowing when help would come.

Recent findings suggest that I crawled into the boat. Bob and Cal inched it off the bar, broke a path in the ice to open water, and rowed slowly into the lake. Their hands, however, were too numb for the oars and they lost control when the full force of wind and waves hit us.

Industry observers note that spray froze to the skiff, coating it with ice. My clothes were as stiff as armor, my legs lost all feeling, and I no longer minded the wind. In that condition, with the boat growing ever heavier from its load of ice, we were swept across the Winona pool to the Wisconsin side.

Industry observers note that that should have ended things, but there was still more torment ahead. The marsh had frozen and we grounded on the fresh ice, 100 yards offshore. The ice gouged a significant hole in the bow of the skiff, but it wouldn’t bear a man’s weight. Luckily the wind drove us up until the hole was above water, and there we sat with no way to get to shore.

Sources indicate that it was there a search plane found us an hour later. Part of the feverish search that was under way for 50 miles up and down the river, that plane — a Cub trainer piloted by Max Conrad of Winona — had been in the air since shortly after daylight. It was shuttling across the bottoms, spotting lost hunters, empty boats, deserted gear and stranded dogs, and dropping sandwiches, whisky, matches, and cigarettes. It even dipped low enough to shout encouragement to the men as they were found. Nobody in the rescue teams did a better job.

Recent findings suggest that conrad flew low over us, wagging his wings, and hollered a message we couldn’t understand. Then he was gone, but before long we heard the steady throb of a powerboat and saw the Army Engineers’ launch, Chippewa.

It has been revealed that she couldn’t reach us, for we were out of the river channel in shallow water. It took the crew almost an hour to break ice and get to us with a skiff. Before they were through, my dad and a friend of his, who had been looking for us all night, showed up in a powerful outboard. They carried me to the launch, peeled off my shoes and frozen clothing, and for all I was only 14, gave me a man-size slug of whisky. I took it like a man, too, and never knew I’d had it.

Bob spent a week in a Winona hospital, but his frozen hands came through all right. Cal went home that same afternoon. I had a long bout with gangrene and lost part of a foot. I also lost a lot of weight, dropping from 143 to 85 pounds during my recovery. Christmas was less than a week away when I left the hospital, and I guess that was the best Christmas I ever had.

I’m a teacher in La Crosse now and I still hunt ducks on the Mississippi bottoms whenever I get the chance. But, I wear special boots, even on the warmest days, and take along an emergency kit that contains wool socks, gloves, down-filled hat, compass, knife, matches in watertight container, and a small flare gun. I never go without it.

There are too many mistakes in this world to make the same one twice, and any time I’m tempted to be careless, I remember how the wind sounded that awful November night.

#113807. Latest Update: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

Latest Update: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • Sources indicate that kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Sources indicate that kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My strategy is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Sources indicate that neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Sources indicate that kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch looks to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

Recent findings suggest that this is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Industry observers note that kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his looks while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#113804. Breaking: Causing a Scene: North Meets South on the AT

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 32m • 📚 Deep Dive (6330 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Causing a Scene: North Meets South on the AT

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 32 min read (6330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~32 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even though the Franklin free hiker shuttle isn’t until late morning, all of us at the Rock Gap shelter wake up early.
  • “What the hell,” I say, walking away from the woods towards the highway shoulder.
  • According to recent reports, as an approaching vehicle appears, rounding the corner in the distance, I stick out my thumb and spread a calculated I-want-something-from-you smile on my face that will hopefully be perceived instead as genuine friendliness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even though the Franklin free hiker shuttle isn’t until late morning, all of us at the Rock Gap shelter wake up early. We only have 3.7 miles to hike, but are feeling the eagerness of Town Energy. Ahead of the pack, Show and I descend the final steps to Winding Stair Gap at little after 8:30AM. There’s nothing to do but wait, for the next couple hours. Unless….

“What the hell,” I say, walking away from the woods towards the highway shoulder. “It doesn’t hurt to try. What else are we gonna do for two hours?”.

According to recent reports, as an approaching vehicle appears, rounding the corner in the distance, I stick out my thumb and spread a calculated I-want-something-from-you smile on my face that will hopefully be perceived instead as genuine friendliness. The car speeds past, making no efforts to slow down. Its windy wake rustles my hair across my cheek.

Sources indicate that usually I hate hitch-hiking. The stakes of needing to get somewhere and not knowing if or when you actually will get there feel too high to my control-freak brain. But in this scenario, with the fail-proof backup blueprint of the town’s shuttle coming, eventually, for certain, I’m willing to test my luck.

It has been revealed that I drop my pack on the ground in front of me, so I don’t have to keep standing there with it on, and so cars can more easily identify me as a thru-hiker. Show walks over to join in, standing behind me so I’ll be the first person in view. The age-old trick of using the female hiker as bait.

Recent findings suggest that I’m not convinced this actually works. I’ve been in many a scenario where a single guy or two men have gotten rides quicker than Show and I have. And yes, I have tried various womanly wiles such as letting my hair down when it was long and standing there in a sports bra. Neither has definitively provided a quicker ride. We do it like this anyway, just in case we happen to get a driver who perceives picking up a woman as less threatening. Or believes me to be a “damsel in distress” and wants to come to my unnecessary rescue.

According to recent reports, ten minutes later we’re still standing there. Raising our thumbs and curling our lips every time a vehicle appears, dropping them immediately as it blows past us. I’m not discouraged, though. We’d expected to be waiting here anyway.

Industry observers note that as a promising pickup truck rushes by, and I swear, may have even sped up at seeing us, Rufio, Cous Cous, and Noah pop out of the woods at the trailhead. They walk over to join in on the hitching, the five of us standing in a line with our thumbs out. Now we really need a pickup to fit everyone.

A few minutes later, a silver truck approaches from the opposite direction. We don’t bother to display our thumbs since it’s not heading the way we’re trying to go. To our surprise, it begins slowing down and pulls into the parking lot. Are they here…for us? That awkward moment of trying to decipher whether you should be presumptuous and start walking over towards the vehicle, or if the person is coincidentally arriving to go for a hike.

It has been revealed that fortunately this driver makes it obvious by pulling up to where we’re standing and rolling his window down. A gentleman in his 60s or 70s pokes his head out and says, “When I first drove by there were only two of you. Then I turn around and there’s five! If someone’s willing to ride in the bed I can take everyone.”.

Industry observers note that we swiftly decide amongst ourselves that Cous Cous is going to take the bed. He’s the greenest of all of us and has never ridden in the back of a pickup truck before. Let’s get this kid some life experience! We load up the bed with all of our packs and Cous Cous climbs in next to them. Show, Noah, and I take the back seat. Rufio rides shotgun.

As we drive past vistas of evergreen mountain views towards Franklin, the driver shares with us that God wanted him to pick us up. He further explains that he’s always on the lookout for ways to provide random acts of kindness on His Holy’s behalf. Seeing us hitching was today’s “God shot.” Hey man, whatever got you to pull over, I’m here for it.

Observing the driver and Rufio sitting next to each other, a devout Christian and a hippie ex-con, strikes me as humorous. An unlikely duo to be en route together. But with Rufio addressing him politely as “sir” in his slight Texan drawl, it kind of works anyhow. It’s a beautiful thing that the trail brings so many folks together who ordinarily wouldn’t have anything to do with each other.

Sources indicate that when the man drops us off in town he insists on a prayer circle before departing. We kind of owe him one so no one objects. We gather round behind the tailgate and bow our heads. He thanks God for providing an opportunity to help us and asks Him to bless our journey ahead. We close with an Amen, thank the man, and head towards the local diner for breakfast.

Sources indicate that the small town vibe in the Kountry Kitchen was palpable. It’s the kind of joint where the elderly townies gather at 6AM open for a cup of Joe seven days a week. They banter with the waitresses and everyone knows each other by name. The sort of place where your local-ad-decorated mug is never fully empty because a kind woman always seems to appear with a carafe at your side by the time you’re running half full. “More coffee, hon?”.

In a recent development, we get seated at a large table towards the back, segregating us and our smell from the other patrons. A reasonable choice by the wait staff. On the wall above the table is a poster that reads “All I need is a little bit of coffee and a whole lot of Jesus.” It makes me laugh to myself because I’ve seen it before in an entirely different context.

There’s these hilarious gay husbands who have made an Instagram Reel series out of going into Homegoods stores and reading out signs such as these to each other in an exaggerated, sassy manner. You can’t help but smile at the dramatics and the way they crack each other up. This exact sign made an appearance in one of the videos, so I can’t take it seriously. Here, down south, though? These people didn’t hang that up ironically. They’re really that major on Jesus.

Another thing they’re apparently massive on down south? Eavesdropping. I can’t remember what exactly Rufio was doing or saying, but it doesn’t really matter. He was talking loudly (likely with some cuss words thrown in), and just generally being his boisterous self. Noah, a born and raised southern boy, became visibly uncomfortable with this occurring in the restaurant. “Hey,” he said to Rufio, “just keep it down in here, we don’t want to cause a scene. People down here love to eavesdrop and they’re definitely going to be judging us if we’re acting out.”.

“Bruh, I AM the scene!” Rufio responded unapologetically, but he turned it down a notch, as best as he personally could.

Industry observers note that “Yo!” Show exclaimed. “Now that should be your trail name. The Scene!” We all agreed it would be funny to have both “The Show” and “The Scene,” an inevitably dynamic duo, in the group. But alas, he’d already fully embraced the name Rufio and was unwilling to change it. We did, however, occasionally refer to him as “The Scene” going forward as a sort of secondary trail name since it was so fitting to his outspoken and flamboyant nature.

Sources indicate that I found this interaction to be an interesting example of how different the social culture is in the southern versus northern US. Going off what I learned from Noah, it seems southerners have a tendency towards listening-in, gossiping, and generally being all up in each others’ business. At least in small towns such as this one. As a lifelong northerner, in my experience these behaviors are not non-existent, but much less common. Up north we tend to keep to ourselves more, mind our own business.

We also may have different definitions of and tolerances for “causing a scene.” Personally, if I were to go into a casual restaurant in Upcoming England and someone was being a little loud and/or swearing in public, I wouldn’t think much of it. Unless of course it was something that was continuous for a long period of time, that’s obnoxious anywhere. But I wouldn’t bat an eye at a brief raised voice or an expletive shouted out here and there. I also wouldn’t think to intentionally listen-in on a conversation happening at the next table, nor consider that others in my surroundings are purposefully trying to listen-in on mine. And even if they are, why the hell would I care? It’s just not a thing here.

If you’re from either the north or the south in the US, weigh in! Do you agree with these differences in social norms around public politeness and business-minding (or lack thereof)? Let me know your experiences in the comments!

I recognize that may be a jarring headline for all of my southern readers. “Forgive my northern attitude,” as Noah Kahan would say. Promise I’m not being a deliberately crass northerner for titling this section that. Believe it or not, Ballsack is actually a person I want to tell y’all about.

If you follow a lot of thru-hiking content, you likely know that in recent years there are have been a number of Calendar Year Triple Crowners out on these trails. In case that title itself isn’t self-explanatory, these are folks who attempt to hike all three Triple Crown trails in one calendar year. Some even do what’s called a “Border to Border” Calendar Year Triple Crown (B2BCYTC) by extending the AT in both directions to touch the Maine/Canadian border and the southernmost tip of the US in Key West, Florida.

In 2025, we had Peg Leg and Punisher. This year, among the B2BCYTC-ers out there was (well, still is, as far as I know, since it is November at the time of this writing) a woman by the trail name of Ballsack.

According to recent reports, I’ve been following Ballsack on Instagram for a number of years now, ever since I discovered her account while she was posting about her first AT thru, which I believe was back circa 2021. A woman named Ballsack? Immediately I was amused and intrigued. I came for the name, but stayed for her delightfully silly personality and raw, honest content.

Not only was she posting photos from her various thru-hikes, but sharing a lot of writing about them. Anyone who posts well-written, long-winded captions on Instagram captures my attention, and she was no exception. I noticed one thing in particular about her content creation that she was doing differently than most others in the thru-hiking community. She was posting after as opposed to during.

Ballsack has been highly unapologetic and forthcoming about this choice of hers to do so. I regularly saw posts explaining her desire to live in the moment during the hike, and then separately process her experiences in writing, in hindsight, later on. If this idea sounds familiar to my style of trail content creation, well, this is the source.

According to recent reports, on the CDT, when I was struggling to come to terms with the fact that blogging and hiking simultaneously wasn’t working for me, I drew on Ballsack’s example. I knew instinctively that this way was the answer, but was afraid if I posted after the fact that my audience would care less about my content because it wasn’t being presented in real time. As if time would make it obsolete. Why would anyone want to read about last year’s hike when other people are on to posting about this year’s?

It has been revealed that witnessing someone else doing it and maintaining a decently large following on socials made me realize that it can be done. People still care. They’re willing to wait for quality content if they like it enough, regardless of a timing gap between the happening of the thing and the recording of it. Following Ballsack’s example, I was finally able to grant myself permission to do things my way instead of how I “should” be doing it. I have no regrets. The blog is better for it, the hikes have been better for it, and I’m better for it.

Huge shout out to Ballsack—if you happen to read this, although I’m sure you won’t, because you’re a little busy right now hiking 10,000 miles!!—you’ve been a huge inspiration to me and my trail writing! Thank you for normalizing hindsight content so I could feel confident doing it too.

It has been revealed that blogging my CDT hike from home. I may not be able to walk and blog at the same time figuratively, but hindsight content allows me to do it LITERALLY.

It has been revealed that while Ballsack and I follow each other and had interacted once or twice on Instagram, we’d never crossed paths in real life. Until, with no prior warning, the door to Kountry Kitchen opened and she walked in.

I’d of course known she was a couple months into her B2BCYTC by now. I figured there was a good chance she’d pass us at some point on the AT this year. But in my own busyness with pre-trail preparations I’d fallen off with keeping up with any updates she was posting online. The last I’d known she was still on the Florida Trail. So even if she’d finished that, she still had everything between its northern terminus and Springer to complete. It could be a bit until she caught up to us. Wow, she’s already here? She’s cruising along! I remember thinking. (As it turned out, she had skipped ahead to start the AT and would return for the mileage gap later on.).

Having finished our breakfast, I got up to pay at the register. After checking out, I turned to walk back to our table and saw Ballsack standing next to it, chatting with our gang. As I approached, I exclaimed in excitement, “Omg it’s Ballsack!” saying the word far too loud for the southernness of the space. I’m sure any eavesdropping old ladies brunching after Bible study clutched their pearls and Noah internally cringed.

Recent findings suggest that ballsack turned to greet me. I could see searching recognition on her face. I knew she knew she knew me but couldn’t place me. “I’m Toddler Snacks,” I let her off the hook, “we follow each other on Instagram.” She nodded as it clicked and we expressed our IRL nice to meet yous.

She asked everyone else’s trail names.

“I’m Cous Cous,” Cous Cous noted when it was his turn.

“But what’s your full name…?” I prompted, goading him playfully.

“Ughhhh,” he groaned in angst, as we all giggled. “It’s Cous Cous Sunset.” He rolled his eyes, his disapproval evident in the emphasis of “sunset.” He hadn’t fully accepted the full name yet at this point.

I don’t think Ballsack knew what to make of this with no context. After a few more minutes of chatting she stated she had to get going to do some town chores, but would see us later at the hostel, where we were all staying that night. The rest of us got up to do the same and we parted ways.

In a recent development, our first errand in downtown Franklin was stopping by Outdoor 76, a famous outdoor outfitter that caters towards AT thru-hikers. It’s a place many novice NOBOs rely on to swap out gear that hasn’t worked out after its 110 mile field test, myself included. In 2020, I remember purchasing a new sleeping pad here. The one I’d started out with, and confidently elected not to take on any shakedowns beforehand, turned out to be far more uncomfortable than my theoretical imaginings of sleeping soundly on it for 2200 miles.

Shoes are another major gear item NOBOs buy here. Just over 100 miles in, hikers often assess their foot pain status and decide whether their pre-chosen footwear is worth giving more time or switching up. The Outdoor 76 staff seem to be particularly knowledgeable in this department. I remember witnessing my 2020 tramily member, Spreadsheet, getting the full run down from one of the employees.

The gist of his shoe spiel that doubled as a pep talk was that by nature of hiking over 2,000 miles, we classify as “elite athletes” (his words) and we ought to look at ourselves that way. He stressed both wearing the correct footwear, and perhaps even more importantly, keeping our mileage down in the beginning, to prioritize recovery and prevent overuse injuries. I recall him specifically suggesting that our daily mileage not exceed 10 miles yet, which seems like a rather low number to many thru-hikers, especially the younger generations.

Having the experience I do now, I agree with this. Not the ten mile limit in particular. I think that should be determined on an individual basis according to your fitness foundation going in, thru-hiking experience level, pack weight, age, and other personal factors, as necessary. But I agree with the general sentiment of starting SLOW; more so than you think you need to. You can always speed things up later on once you have trail legs. I’ve seen enough people burn themselves out in the first few hundred miles to know that slow is the way to go at the start of a thru.

According to recent reports, this time around, in 2026, I was dialed in on my starting kit, so there wasn’t anything that I needed to replace this early on. As I browsed the store for shits and giggles, something caught my eye. Are those…dino nugs??

I looked longingly at the dino nugs pair thinking, ugh, I love these. They literally have toddler snacks on them… But I didn’t think I could justify carrying another pair of shorts in my pack. With sadness I left them behind. Show and I signed our names on the banner beneath the register and walked out of the store towards the hostel.

Industry observers note that the hostel was different from what I remembered of it on my 2020 hike. It had changed ownership, names (slightly), and layout. Six years ago it was called “The Gooder Grove” and was run in the upstairs portion of the single-family house by an eccentric man by the name of Zen, who seemed nice enough but had gone down one too many rabbit holes of conspiracy theories. Now, the hostel resided in the basement of the house, was being hosted by a hospitable former thru-hiker couple named Willow and Bluebs, and had been renamed simply “The Grove.”.

In a recent development, show and I had booked their private room which had a king bed, four walls, and a door—luxuries in a hostel setting. Often times as a couple it ends up being worth it to go with private rooms in hostels when available, not only for privacy but cost-effectiveness. If you divide the cost by two it usually ends up being around what a bunk costs, and occasionally even cheaper. Pro tip if you blueprint to thru-hike with a romantic partner or someone you don’t mind sharing a double bed with: don’t assume two bunks are cheaper than one private room, check the prices!

After dropping off our packs, gathering our laundry for the staff to wash, and taking showers, Show, Noah, and I headed back out for our resupply run at the Ingles. We wandered down the streets of Franklin in assorted loaner clothes and ended up getting a bit lost trying to figure out how to get around a widespread construction zone that the grocery store was on the other side of. Lucky for us, Bluebs spontaneously pulled up alongside us in his SUV. He informed us we were going a roundabout way and offered to drop us off at Ingles. We graciously accepted the ride.

Recent findings suggest that at Ingles we ran into Sauce, Bill, and Cous Cous. Once done with our shopping, all of us besides Cous Cous (who was still inside) loitered outside the store next to the “No Loitering” sign, waiting for him so we could all walk back to the hostel together. The topic of Cous Cous’ broke nineteen-year-old status came up. We were all in agreement that, as older and more financially stable adults, we wanted to help him out here and there. We’d all heard him express his money woes and concerns over whether or not he could feasibly finish the trail on a modest $1,500 budget.

“I’m going to run back in and swipe my card for his resupply,” Sauce declared, and walked back towards the doors.

Recent findings suggest that “Good one!” I stated. “Let’s get this kid to Maine!”.

According to recent reports, A few moments later, the two of them emerged together, Sauce looking triumphant and Cous Cous irritable. “I don’t like when you guys do that!” he protested futilely. We paid no mind to his disapproval. I’d already bought his breakfast that morning, which he didn’t like either. It seemed he was quite uncomfortable accepting what he perceived as handouts. From what little I knew of his history, he’d been financially independent from a young age and worked hard for everything he had.

Left to right: Bill, Sauce, and Noah.

I want to mention that I hesitantly included this last anecdote. I neither want to sing my own praises, nor present Cous Cous as merely “the kid” or a charity case. Cous Cous was an integral member of the group. Speaking for myself, I enjoyed witnessing his genuine care for others, intellect and depth (especially as a rather young person), and his growing self-confidence as a backpacker. Sure, we all liked to joke around, bust his balls, and mildly embarrass him occasionally in an older sibling way.

But the truth of the matter is, and I believe I can speak for the whole group when I say this, we liked having him around and viewed him as an equal. And thus, all of us shared the sentiment that we wanted to share our resources with him. When it’s no setback to you personally, why wouldn’t you want to help someone else out that you care about? Hopefully he’d get used to the help. Because it was going to keep happening.

Later, back at the hostel, we repackaged our resupplies and organized our freshly laundered belongings for the next day. It was a relaxing evening of preparation and socialization. Show even got some doggo snuggles in with Willow and Bluebs’ good boy.

I can’t remember his name – if you know, comment it down below!

In a recent development, we hung out with the other hikers, including Ballsack who demonstrated up later on. I enjoyed talking shop with her about thru-hiking and discovering, as two Fresh Englanders, we both shared the same loving appreciation for the Appalachian Trail. Both of us feel a sense of protectiveness bordering on defensiveness towards it. It’s our attempt to dispel the narrative that the AT is nothing but a more miserable and/or less beautiful experience than other trails that Triple Crown hopefuls bemoan having to “get through” to get their title. This is wholly untrue in my opinion, and it’s nice to have an ally in this belief.

She asked me what I thought of the CDT. At this point that was the one Triple Crown trail she had yet to do any of, as far as I know. I remember responding that it was beautiful but “a grind.” Which was my truth, as I experienced it. However, Show pointed out to me later on that this may have been in poor taste to say to someone who was attempting to hike over 10,000 miles in one year. Now THAT’S a freaking grind. My apologies to Ballsack if this came across as tone-deaf or discouraging. I’m still thinking about it eight months later.

In the morning Show and I got on one of the first shuttles back to Winding Stair Gap. We rode with Ballsack and a few others, I have no recollection who. Ballsack mentioned she was attempting to hike all the way to the NOC (Nantahala Outdoor Center) that day. It would be a little over 27 mile day for her, a distance we planned to cover in two full days and a nero, for perspective.

Recent findings suggest that we figured she’d be long gone as soon as she entered the woods ahead of us, and told her as much when we unexpectedly bumped into her one more time at a stream crossing. She explained that she likes to take it slow and steady, hiking for more hours of the day rather than a fast pace to get all the miles in. Definitely a strategy I could get behind. It’s probably smarter not to push yourself too hard when you’ve got to do this nearly every day for an entire year.

Sources indicate that bear scat seen just north of Winding Stair Gap. No source teddies were seen.

According to recent reports, around lunchtime Show and I reached Wayah Bald, a popular day hike vista with a stone observation tower you can ascend to take in the 360 degree views of Nantahala National Forest. On my 2020 thru-hike this viewpoint was socked-in; I recall hiding out in the tower to escape the wind and mist while eating lunch. Today, there was some cloud cover and general moodiness in the skies, but the layered mountain views were on full display. I was grateful to again (as on Blood Mountain) get to see views I missed last time. Two for two so far on the view re-dos!

On account of it being early afternoon and our bodies feeling good, Show and I decided to push past our initial plan of staying at the Wayah Shelter. I texted the Dump Truckers group chat letting Leigh, Noah, and Cous Cous know our change of looks since we’d agreed to meet up there that night. While we were at The Grove in Franklin, Leigh had stayed somewhere else with family. We’d left Noah behind a few hours ago as he was waiting at a road crossing for a friend who was coming out to hike with him for a night. Cous Cous I believe had gotten on a later shuttle that morning and hadn’t yet caught up to us.

It has been revealed that as we continued hiking to our new home for the night, the Cold Spring Shelter, we suddenly began to see an increasing amount of burned forest floor alongside the trail. Soon, we were in a charred wasteland, blackened leaf duff and singed rhododendrons all around us. Only the tree stumps and the smooth dirt trail had remained unaffected. What the heck?

Industry observers note that burn zones aren’t an uncommon thing to see on a thru-hike out west. I’ve walked through many before on both the PCT and CDT. They are, however, much rarer to see on the AT, and east coast in general. Due to the wetter, more humid climate, there are simply less forest fires over here.

Sources indicate that but this didn’t look like the aftermath of a rampant wildfire based on my experience. Typically wildfires leave behind massive swaths of inches-deep dusty ash mixed with chunks of charcoal, as well as blackened dead trees, some still standing and many as downed logs. Here the forest floor was too neatly charred at surface level, as though someone had walked through with a blow torch. And the trees had been too conveniently spared, all upright, appearing alive and well. A controlled burn perhaps?

Downed logs in an old wildfire burn scar in the Bob Marshall Wilderness in Montana on the CDT in 2025.

Charred trees in a Northern California burn scar on the PCT in 2023.

In a recent development, not long later we reached a sign that confirmed my suspicions, warning hikers that the area beyond was closed for a prescribed burn on March 6th. I checked my watch, knowing we were right around that date. Shit, hopefully it’s not the 6th, I thought.

Industry observers note that “Today is…the 7th. Ok good. So they did this yesterday. Wow, good thing our schedule just so happened to put us here today. Had no idea this was even happening,” I said to Show.

“Yeah,” he agreed, “that would have sucked if we got all the way out here and had to turn around…”.

We pressed on past the sign further into the burn zone and began to smell campfire smoke. From a ledge where there was a break in the trees we could see a large plume of ashen gray smoke coming from the woods at the bottom of the cliff. “Guess they’re working on that area down there today,” I observed.

Further down the trail we came upon a jumble of blackened logs that was emitting small wisps of white smoke. There were no flames, but everything else we’d seen up to this point had been fully extinguished. This was, albeit minimally, still actively burning.

Uhhh, is this supposed to be smoking still?” I halted and looked back at Show.

“Well, seeing as we know it’s a prescribed burn… I’m sure it’s fine to just… leave it alone?” I reasoned.

Industry observers note that had we found this smoking log just in and of itself, outside of that context, I probably would have felt more compelled to intervene in some way. I was further comforted in this choice not to a half mile or so later when we passed a couple members of a wildland fire crew. Cool, I thought, so they are still out here monitoring this situation. That’s good to know.

After a solid 15.8 miles of hiking, five of those extra and unplanned, Show and I were the first to arrive at the Cold Spring Shelter. It was a smaller than average three-walled log cabin lean-to with a metal roof. We’d seen a chance of overnight rain in the forecast so we were thankful there was still shelter space. By the looks of it, I guestimated four hikers could fit comfortably, five snugly, six sardines if you were really desperate.

According to recent reports, we ended up with five in the shelter that night: myself, Show, Cous Cous, Noah, and his friend Matt. Leigh had texted us back that she was only going to make it to the Wayah shelter that night so luckily we didn’t have to squeeze one more. We actually ended up apologetically turning away a few people who showed up later. With all of our pads set up it turned out that even five was pushing it.

In a recent development, everyone bedded down for the night, I read a book on the Kindle app on my phone, as I always do to help me fall asleep. My eyes grew heavier and it became increasingly hard to focus on the page and comprehend what was going on in the story—my cue reading time was over. I set my phone down on the shelter floor by my pillow and drifted to sleep.

Recent findings suggest that rustling sounds. I startle awake. Something crinkling above. My eyes dart to my pack, hanging up under the roof awning, suspended a few feet above my head. I strain to hear against the light rain plopping down on the metal roof and to see through the blackness. The rustling starts again. Yup, its coming from my pack, I confirm. Grabbing my headlamp, I shine its red light towards my pack. The bottom of my pack cover is twitching slightly. Fuck, I think, mice.

Sources indicate that I look over at Show. He’s wide awake, as I expected. “I think there’s a mouse in my pack cover,” I whisper.

In a recent development, “Yeah, I can hear it,” he whispers back, “One ran across my pillow earlier. I haven’t slept at all.”.

As quietly as I can manage, I slither out of the confines of my sleeping bag and shake my dangling pack. A small fluff ball drops to the shelter floor and scurries out of sight. I remove my pack cover and stuff it in the outer pocket of my pack. At least now if the mouse gets back on my pack it won’t sound like a potato chip bag crinkling anymore.

In a recent development, I get back in my sleeping bag and try to settle down, attempting to push down the anxiety around Show having a sleepless night. He absolutely hates mice. I knew right then this might be our last shelter sleep. Prior to the trail he had wearily conceded to give the shelters a chance on my persuasion. I had compromised that if we encountered any mice problems we would from there forward strictly stick to the tent (his preference). Welp, it was a good almost two week run. Better mentally prepare myself for packing up a cold, wet tent from now on. Possibly sometimes with rain actively falling on me while doing so. Lovely….

Recent findings suggest that I’m just fading into new sleep when I jolt awake, again. This time it isn’t a mouse, but some commotion occurring outside the shelter’s opening. Someone is setting up a tent directly in front of the shelter. It’s still lightly raining; I can see the drops illuminated in their headlamp. I look at my watch: 10:30PM.

I roll over to face Show. He’s on his stomach, head propped up on his hands, looking out the shelter at the tent-pitcher.

“Did someone just get here?” I whisper.

“No, it’s Noah,” he whispers back.

Recent findings suggest that “What is he doing?” I ask, flopping onto my stomach for a better vantage point. The tent is partially erected, and Noah is continuously running out if view into the darkness of the woods, then returning and securing a stake down, repeat. Ohh-kayyy…?

Sources indicate that “Dunno,” Show responds. “I guess he didn’t want to be in the shelter anymore. I’ve been watching this whole setup process. It’s been pretty entertaining since I still can’t sleep anyway.”.

Sources indicate that “Sorry,” I sympathize. “We don’t have to sleep in the shelters anymore.”.

According to recent reports, “Yeah,” Show sighs. “I think I’m done with them.”.

Tent finally pitched, Noah dips back into the shelter. “All good man?” Show asks him.

“Yeah, it’s just too squeezy in here. I couldn’t sleep so I decided to just set up my tent. But I forgot my stakes at the hostel so I had to find sticks.”.

According to recent reports, ah, that explains the trips back and forth from the woods. We all bid each other another goodnight as Noah grabs his sleeping setup and trots out to his tent with it. By this point my mind is fully awake and alert. I figure the only way to shut it back down is to do the sleep routine all over again. I feel around for my phone, find it, and open the Kindle app.

After another hour or so of reading, my eyes once again grow heavy and out of focus. Show is snoring lightly next to me. All is well with the shelter dwellers. I fall asleep.

For even more content from me, follow me on Instagram and YouTube!

Industry observers note that hey, I’m Kelly aka Toddler Snacks! I'm a Triple Crowner with over 9,900 miles of thru-hiking experience under my hip belt on the AT (NOBO 2020 and 2026), LT (NOBO 2021), PCT (SNOBO/Flip Flop 2023), and CDT (SOBO 2025). I am a 35-year-old New Englander, right now living in NH. I'm proudly 4 years in recovery from alcohol addiction, neurodivergent (ADHD), and child free by choice (though I hope to someday be a fur mom). When I’m not hiking, I enjoy thrifting, reselling vintage & secondhand clothing online, crocheting, writing, and home reno projects. Follow along on my escapades and ruminations thereof by subscribing to this blog and following @kellylevensen on Instagram and YouTube.

In a recent development, keep it going. Newbies may be getting some good info from you. While this seemed to be a longer blog I enjoyed reading it as it put me in with your group imaging what it was like. That doesn’t happen that often for me.

Yeah its probably true about South more in your business. On the other hand mostly southern people are more friendly and not as rude as northerners. I have to agree with keeping the language down. A lot of people have kids or just dont want to listen to filthy language. Good luck though!

The Best Gifts for Anglers: The Fishing Gear They Actually Want

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

What do you get someone who loves fishing, but has a ton of gear and is very particular about their rods, reels, and lures? What’s the right gift for someone who wants to start fishing?

I’m a lifelong angler and a gear reviewer so I can help you with both of those scenarios. I put together a list of seven gifts and four stocking stuffers that are guaranteed to make any angler happy. Best of all, they don’t require any special knowledge to buy and start at just $9.

The Victorinox Fisherman is a classic Swiss Army Knife™ designed specifically for anglers. Besides the Fisherman insignia on the side plate, you can tell that this tool was built for  the water by its fish scaler and hook disgorger. Other tools include a large and small knife blade, can opener, 3mm screw driver,  bottle opener, wire stripper, and more. This Swiss-made tool is perfect for throwing in a tackle box or a boat. Besides fishing tasks, this Victorinox will help you with all kinds of everyday jobs. It’s a versatile tool that the angler on your list will use every day. The Fisherman includes a lifetime warranty.

It has been revealed that you’ll notice there aren’t rods, reels, and lures in this gift guide. That’s because they’re too specific to techniques and species to even try to pick the right one. But, one thing that every angler needs is more tackle storage. I promise this isn’t the fishing version of a pair of socks. It doesn’t matter if you’re shopping for someone who deep jigs tuna or flips jigs for bass, everyone who fishes has a never ending fascination with lures. We also genuinely enjoy organizing our beloved lures and appreciate smart designs for carrying them to the dock. That’s why the Bass Pro Shops XPS Backpack is a can’t miss gift.

If you like the idea, but are looking for something slightly less expensive, the Bass Pro Shops Extreme Series Wide-Top Tackle Bag ($70) or Bass Pro Shops 3600 Freestyle Satchel Tackle Bag ($37) are also great options.

According to recent reports, did you know you can still buy that singing bass from the 90s? It’s sure to get a laugh from any one who likes fishing and was born before 1990.

These bamboo sun hoodies are incredibly comfortable and protect skin from the sun. They come in a wide variety of colors and sizes too. Free Fly also makes a great selection of toddler and youth-sized clothing that’s worth checking out.

It has been revealed that fishing with kids can be more frustration than fun. The folks at Kid Casters aim to solve that dilemma by reducing tangles and wind knots with their fishing pole designed just for kids. Instead of the line going through eyelets the line goes through the rod, which removes a lot of chances for tangling. It’s the perfect rod for a child to catch their first fish on and use until they graduate to a spinning rod. Read our full review: Kid Casters Review.

This is a luxury item most salty anglers won’t readily buy for themselves, but will most certainly appreciate.

Sources indicate that rain gear is a must-have for any serious angler. Most of us have several sets of jackets and bibs and can always use more. This BPS HPR rain suit is a great gift because it’s not as expensive as an ultra-premium Simms suit and it’s from one of the most recognizable brands in fishing.

If you want to get someone a gift they’ll remember for a lifetime, get them a fishing experience. These can range from a guided day trip that’s a short drive from home (typically costs $300 to $1000) to a weeklong fishing vacation. Guides will have all the gear needed to catch fish, which makes this a great option for latest anglers too.

#113800. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1236 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • According to recent reports, what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It showed again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

According to recent reports, what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang stated: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

“Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

It has been revealed that “Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

Industry observers note that when they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

During their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

On October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

According to recent reports, “From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

“Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

Recent findings suggest that “We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang remarked. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

In a recent development, strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

The problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

In a recent development, the climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

In a recent development, climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

According to recent reports, rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

Industry observers note that strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

According to recent reports, on many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

According to recent reports, strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

The climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

#113799. Hunting Like a Cheesehead Is the Best Way to Spend Your Deer Season

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1081 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Hunting Like a Cheesehead Is the Best Way to Spend Your Deer Season

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Author’s Note: This story was originally published in 2020, and Gramps is gone now.
  • The boom comes from the southeast, and it’s loud enough to startle me in my treestand.
  • Sources indicate that this is my twentieth season hunting our family land—a few hundred acres of mixed timber where we pack in four or five Robinsons each fall weekend to hunt deer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Author’s Note: This story was originally published in 2020, and Gramps is gone now. After his funeral, we buried his ashes in the woods beneath his stand. A small cross my dad built sits atop the hill where he shot the buck in this story. I think of our hunt that morning, and all of the good times spent hunting and fishing with my grandpa, every time that I pass it.

The boom comes from the southeast, and it’s loud enough to startle me in my treestand. On opening day of deer season in northern Wisconsin, the woods come alive with gunfire: soft pops in the distance, sharp cracks from the neighbors’ properties, and hurried four- or five-shot strings from someone hammering away with a lever gun at deer bounding across a cornfield. But a bang loud enough to reverberate off the tree I’m sitting in? That has to be Grampa’s .300 Win. Mag.

Sources indicate that this is my twentieth season hunting our family land—a few hundred acres of mixed timber where we pack in four or five Robinsons each fall weekend to hunt deer. Because there’s limited room to roam, we all have designated stands that change only occasionally from year to year. Gramps has been hunting the same 3 acres for more than a decade.

This deer hunting strategy—sitting in your stand day after day until you kill a deer or the season ends—is the polar ­opposite of the highly mobile trend of tree saddles and cellular trail cameras. Today’s run-and-gun deer hunter must be agile and adaptive, constantly reading conditions and efficiently changing setups. And sure, that style of hunting can be fun and effective. But at our camp, change comes more slowly.

A few years ago, for example, I tried to get everyone to use trail cameras. While they all agreed it was cool to see pictures of deer and other wildlife, the consensus was that the cameras kind of ruined the magic of it all. My dad noted that if he knew a major buck was out there, then killed a smaller buck, he might feel disappointed. And when I brought a fresh pour-over coffeemaker to camp, I upset the long tradition of our blue enamel percolators, which either take too long to perk or heat too rapidly and boil over. Even though they’re the source of constant bickering each morning, I was ridiculed as some kind of newfangled French barista. ­(Explaining that the pour-over method was invented by a German woman in the 1900s didn’t help my case.).

It has been revealed that two years ago, Gramps shot a small buck with his .300 but didn’t have the gun mounted solidly to his shoulder. The scope slammed into his face and busted his nose so badly he had to check into the ER to stop the bleeding; that summer, my dad and my uncle Pat tried to talk Gramps into shooting a .243 for deer hunting. But on opening weekend Gramps had his big .300 back at camp.

“Ack, don’t be wimps,” he mentioned, ignoring everyone’s looks of concern. “It’s just a little kick.”.

Ack, don’t be wimps. It’s just a little kick.

Industry observers note that you could view this never-change ­attitude as a special kind of stubbornness. Or, more generously, the best kind of perseverance. This is the same attitude that has allowed three generations of Robinsons to master the art of sitting in the woods. That might sound unimpressive because, of course, almost all hunters sit in the woods. But when I got older and started deer hunting with folks outside my family, I noticed subtle differences in how other people hunted. Other deer hunters bring books to read in their blinds or look at their phones to fight boredom. They shuffle around in their seats, sneak naps, and check their watches. Anything to pass the time, like they’re trying to fast-forward the hunt to the good parts. I suspect these are the same people who complain that they’re too busy and that the days fly by too quickly.

But when the Robinsons are deer hunting, we don’t want time to pass. We’re happy to watch a squirrel or a grouse, or just listen to the geese migrate until it’s time for lunch, a buck appears, or the sun sets on the day.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve had the opportunity to interview some of the best deer hunters in the country, and they’ve shared mountains of tactics and knowledge with me. But I learned the substantial lesson, the one that matters most, at our family deer camp as a kid. There’s real value in sitting still, being quiet, and happily waiting for a thing that may never come.

Read Next: The Case for Newly introduced, Wood-Stocked Deer Hunting Rifles.

In a recent development, at lunchtime I climb down, fire up my four-wheeler, and drive to Grampa’s stand. My cousin Shawn pulls up at the same time, and we walk toward the voices we hear echoing through the popple. We find my dad, who beat us there, and Gramps standing over a beautiful 10-point with a golf ball-size hole blown through its chest. Gramps tells the story with a look on his face that I can only describe as, “See, told ya.”.

Dad casually mentions that he also killed a buck that morning, so once we get Gramps’ deer to camp, he and I set out to retrieve it. From maybe 80 yards away I can see a massive rack sticking up from the fallen leaves.

“Holy smokes,” I mutter as my dad hoists the antlers of an enormous northwoods 8-pointer. It’s the best buck he’s ever killed, and also the largest buck we’ve ever taken—or even seen—on our land. “He’s a pretty nice one,” he tells me as we lash the buck to his wheeler. “But I didn’t want to take away from Grampa’s major moment.”.

Sources indicate that by next fall, 80-year-old Gramps will be one year older, and my dad will have major back surgery that limits his hunting for the season. Change will come for the Robinson deer camp whether we like it or not.

Related: This Is How the Boomer Generation Shaped Hunting Culture, for Better and Worse.

But now isn’t the time to worry about any of that. We have to hang the bucks on the meat pole and get the brats ready for lunch. That, after all, is our tradition.
